title: Lisav Eissat forced off eight minutes into his Bristol City debut
dek: The Maccabi Haifa academy graduate's first outing for his new club ended almost as soon as it began, cut short by an injury in a pre-season friendly against Stockport County in Spain, with early indications from Israeli reports that it is not serious.

source.name: Sport1 / Maariv

body: Lisav Eissat's first appearance in a Bristol City shirt lasted barely eight minutes. The defender, unveiled by the Championship club only a week earlier, was forced off early in Friday's pre-season friendly against Stockport County at the Robins' training camp in Alicante. The afternoon soured further as his new side slipped to a 2-0 defeat.

Bristol City confirmed Eissat's arrival from Maccabi Haifa on 10 July on a four-year contract, with the fee officially undisclosed. Israeli reports have put the figure at between €2.2 million and €2.5 million, and say Haifa negotiated a sell-on percentage as well as a bonus should the Robins win promotion to the Premier League.

The club has not yet said what the injury is. Israeli reports indicated Bristol City were awaiting the results of medical checks, with one account describing a blow to the head that required his substitution. The same coverage suggested early signs pointed to nothing serious, though no timescale for his return has been given.
Eissat, 21, joined Maccabi Haifa as a small boy and worked his way through the academy before a season-long loan at Hapoel Hadera hardened him for senior football.

Back at Haifa in 2025-26, the centre-back became a regular, making 33 appearances across the league, cup and Conference League qualifying, scoring once and adding two assists, according to Israeli reports.

His fitness will now be monitored in two countries. Born and raised in Israel, Eissat represented the country at youth level from under-15 through to a single under-21 cap, but chose to play his senior international football for Romania, the country of his mother. He made his Romania debut in October 2025 and has since collected four caps.

Eissat is the fifth signing of Bristol City's summer under new head coach Michael Skubala, following Jed Wallace, Gibson Yah, Sam Greenwood and Sam Tickle, as the club reshapes a squad that fell short of expectations last season. The Alicante camp, which began on 12 July, was intended to give the newcomers minutes together before the Championship campaign.

For Eissat, the setback is an unwelcome pause rather than, on current information, anything worse. The defender left the pitch in Spain with his new supporters still waiting for a proper first look at him, and Bristol City will hope the scans allow him to rejoin preparations quickly enough to fight for a place in their opening-day side.

title: Hapoel Tel Aviv Close In on Former NBA Forward Jacob Toppin
dek: Negotiations with the 26-year-old ex-Knicks and Hawks forward have reportedly advanced, with the club confident he will join for 2026/27 — and his Jewish heritage means he would not count as an import.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's long courtship of Jacob Toppin appears to be nearing a conclusion. According to a Sport 5 report published Friday evening by Noa Poplinger, negotiations between the club and the former New York Knicks and Atlanta Hawks forward have advanced markedly. Figures inside the organisation now believe the 26-year-old will be wearing red for the 2026/27 season.

The appeal is easy to understand. Toppin, who is of Jewish heritage, would not occupy one of the club's foreign-player slots under Israeli league rules — a considerable advantage for a roster builder trying to squeeze maximum talent into a limited quota.

The player, for his part, is said to have expressed a genuine willingness to move to Israel. A club source quoted in the report believes the deal will be completed in time for him to be available from the start of the coming campaign.

Toppin's pedigree is unusual for the Winner League market. Born in Brooklyn in May 2000, the 6ft 9in forward began his college career at Rhode Island before transferring to Kentucky, where he averaged 12.4 points and 6.8 rebounds as a senior.

Undrafted in 2023, he earned a two-way contract with the Knicks, splitting his time between Madison Square Garden and the Westchester Knicks of the G League. He later moved on to Atlanta, where he shuttled between the Hawks and the College Park Skyhawks.

His most recent season ended abruptly. In December 2025 he underwent surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right shoulder, an injury that ruled him out for the remainder of the year, and the Hawks waived him on 15 December.

He has been a free agent since, which explains both his availability to a club of Hapoel's means and the element of calculated risk in the move. A fully recovered Toppin, still in his athletic prime, would be a coup; the club will want assurances on the shoulder before anything is signed.

Basketball supporters will recognise the surname. Jacob's older brother is Obi Toppin, the Indiana Pacers forward who won the NBA Slam Dunk Contest in 2022, and the younger Toppin shares much of the family's explosive athleticism above the rim, even if his NBA minutes were harder to come by.

There is a note of patience in the timing. The report stresses that Hapoel do not expect to complete any signings during the Nine Days, the mourning period in the Jewish calendar that concludes with Tisha B'Av on 23 July, so an announcement, if it comes, is likely to wait until the second half of the month.
The club's interest is not new: the same outlet first connected the two parties in December, and Italian outlet Sportando reported in May that contact had been running for around half a year.

For Hapoel, who finished the Winner League regular season second at 22-4 while Maccabi Tel Aviv marched to a 58th championship, the pursuit fits a clear pattern: closing the gap on their city rivals means recruiting players a tier above the league's usual import market. A forward who was on an NBA roster as recently as December would be exactly that.

Toppin, born 8 May 2000 in Brooklyn, is a 6ft 9in forward who went undrafted out of Kentucky in 2023 and played for the New York Knicks and Atlanta Hawks.
He underwent season-ending surgery on a torn labrum in his right shoulder in December 2025 and was waived by Atlanta on 15 December 2025; he is currently a free agent.

body: Mohamed Salah's summer in limbo may be close to a resolution — if a Thursday-evening claim from France proves accurate. Foot Mercato journalist Santi Aouna reported that the 34-year-old, a free agent since his departure from Liverpool at the end of last season, has reached a verbal agreement to join Beşiktaş.

According to Aouna's report, the Egyptian would move to Istanbul on a free transfer, signing a one-year contract with an option for a second. The package is said to be worth around €10m a season plus roughly €2m in bonuses. Crucially, even the reporting itself describes the arrangement as verbal only: nothing has been signed, and no medical or announcement has been scheduled.

Turkish media paint a slightly more cautious picture. A Spor's Yağız Sabuncuoğlu described the two parties as very close rather than agreed, while Kartal Record, a website with close ties to Beşiktaş, reported an official offer worth up to €12m a year with an automatic extension triggered by appearances. Those accounts also claim Salah trimmed his salary demand from €15m and that a percentage of shirt sales has been discussed.

The reported rationale is that Salah prefers to remain in Europe and to live in a Muslim-majority country, with Turkish outlets adding that his family is keen on settling in Istanbul — considerations said to have moved Beşiktaş ahead of richer suitors in Saudi Arabia and Major League Soccer.

There are, however, substantial reasons for caution. Neither Beşiktaş nor Salah's agent, Ramy Abbas Issa, has confirmed an agreement, and Abbas posted on X that "we still don't know where Mohamed will play next season, but we may know very soon". Fabrizio Romano, the transfer market's most-followed chronicler, has recently reported concrete MLS interest and characterised Saudi Arabia as the likeliest destination; as of Thursday night he had not corroborated any Beşiktaş agreement, and nor had the BBC, Sky Sports, The Guardian or ESPN.

The backdrop is a fractious end to one of the great Premier League careers. Salah's final Liverpool season soured after he lost his starting place, and he told ViaPlay that the club were "throwing me under the bus" — an extraordinary public rupture that preceded his summer exit and left the Premier League's most decorated African player without a club at 34.

Until a first-rank outlet or an official announcement confirms the Istanbul deal, the Foot Mercato claim should be read as exactly that: a single outlet's report on a fast-moving negotiation. With Abbas promising clarity "very soon" and Turkish clubs pushing to conclude business before the season starts, the wait for a definitive answer may be short.

body: Mohammed Abu Fani's first outing in Serbian league football could scarcely have gone better. The Israel midfielder played every minute of Crvena Zvezda's 5-0 demolition of Mačva Šabac on Friday night, as the champions opened their SuperLiga title defence in front of 11,254 spectators at the Rajko Mitić Stadium in Belgrade.

The contest was settled long before halftime. Bruno Duarte opened the scoring in the seventh minute, Rade Krunić headed in a second on 18, and an own goal from Mačva's Issa Kone made it 3-0 at the break. Vasilije Kostov completed the rout with a second-half brace, converting from close range three minutes after the restart and adding a fifth with eight minutes to play.

Abu Fani, stationed alongside Krunić at the base of a 4-2-3-1, was woven into the early surge. Red Star's own match report credited him with the cross that found Duarte for the opener, while B92's account placed his delivery at the start of the move that produced Krunić's header instead. The bookkeeping differs, but every version has the newcomer's touches running through the first-half blitz.
He also drew a save with a 66th-minute strike from distance, turned behind for a corner, and released Nair Tiknizyan down the left with one raking diagonal.

Just as telling was what happened around him. With European qualifying on the horizon, Red Star rotated heavily once the result was safe, making five changes between the 62nd and 75th minutes. Abu Fani was not among those withdrawn, completing the full match in his first competitive league outing for his new club.

The 28-year-old arrived in Belgrade in June from Ferencváros, for a fee Serbian outlets put at around one million euros on a three-year contract — a move widely reported to have been championed by head coach Dejan Stanković. In Budapest he won two Hungarian championships and this year's Hungarian Cup, having left Israel in 2023 as a title winner with Maccabi Haifa after coming through the ranks at Hapoel Hadera.

For Red Star, chasing what Serbian media bill as a tenth successive championship, the evening amounted to a controlled tune-up before Champions League qualifying begins. For Abu Fani, going the distance on opening night reads as an early statement of trust from his new employers — and a promising sign for Israeli supporters tracking his path towards continental football this autumn.

Stanković used his post-match remarks to spell out the licence he has handed his new midfielder. He said he had known precisely what Abu Fani could and could not yet give him — the Israeli is still working back to full fitness — but stressed what he does bring: making the players around him feel good, driving the game, and operating like a classic playmaker.

"Even if he loses the ball, he has my blessing," Stanković said, adding that nothing turns into a drama because he knows Abu Fani will come back and demand the next ball. He called him a very easy player to work with. Red Star now turn to Tuesday's Champions League second qualifying round tie against Larne of Northern Ireland.

title: 'To them, the fans are an ATM': Rapyd chief Shtilman turns on Maccabi Tel Aviv's new owners

body: Arik Shtilman, the co-founder and chief executive of payments company Rapyd and the principal sponsor of Maccabi Tel Aviv's basketball club, has delivered a blistering assessment of the Recanati family only days after they completed the purchase that made them the club's majority owners. "From their perspective, the fans are an ATM that is supposed to fund them," he said on the Israeli podcast Anachnu BaMapa ("We're on the Map"), remarks reported by an Israeli sports outlet on Friday evening.

The criticism is rooted in a takeover battle Shtilman lost. In late May he agreed to acquire half of Fedanco Sports, the Federman family vehicle that held 29 per cent of the club, and with his partners proposed injecting around $30 million — an arrangement always contingent on the other shareholders declining their contractual right to buy the stake themselves.

The Recanati family exercised precisely that right of first refusal. On Wednesday they completed a purchase reported at roughly $50 million, lifting their holding from 29 to 58 per cent and leaving Shtilman outside the ownership structure.

In the podcast he characterised the move as financial opportunism rather than sporting ambition, claiming the family had bought the shares only to flip them at a higher price and that ego and control mattered more to them than the team. He said they feared change and refused to communicate with supporters.

He also gave his own account of a first shareholders' meeting, saying he had pressed for a larger budget while Udi Recanati was the only shareholder to oppose an increase and long-serving chairman Shimon Mizrahi backed him. These are Shtilman's descriptions of private discussions, and none of them has been independently corroborated.

His most concrete claims concerned recruitment. Had the refusal right not been exercised, he argued, Maccabi would probably have secured two frontline centres and a further guard by mid-July, naming Bruno Fernando, Richaun Holmes and Tomas Satoransky among the players who could have arrived, while Mike James and Shane Larkin were discussed but ruled out on basketball grounds.

He further suggested the budget had since been trimmed, linking a drawn-out renewal for Iffe Lundberg to the cost of the Yam Madar signing he says he pushed through. Neither the club nor any of the players named has commented on those assertions.

Shtilman made clear he has no intention of walking away from the sponsorship, under which the team competes as Maccabi Rapyd Tel Aviv on a seven-year agreement, but he promised to be a loud presence. "Rapyd will not remain on the shirt of an uncompetitive EuroLeague team," he said, claiming that roughly 80 per cent of supporters shared his view and vowing to return to the ownership picture sooner than people expect. With an appropriate budget for sporting director Claudio Coldebella and head coach Oded Katash, he argued, a Final Four challenge would be realistic.

The Recanati family were not quoted in response and had made no public reply by the time of publication. Their stated position remains the transaction itself: the business daily Globes has reported that the family intends to invest tens of millions of dollars in the playing budget over the coming years, and Udi Recanati has previously said he prefers to work quietly behind the scenes while Mizrahi speaks for the club. For now, the sharpest public account of Maccabi's boardroom comes from one side of a dispute whose other party has, at least publicly, chosen silence.

In May 2026 Shtilman agreed to acquire 50% of Fedanco Sports, the Federman family vehicle holding 29% of the club, with a proposed investment of around $30 million contingent on other shareholders waiving their purchase rights.

The source report contained no response from the Recanati family; Globes has separately reported the family intends to invest tens of millions of dollars in the playing budget.

body: Rodina Moscow are said to be monitoring Basam Zaarura, with the newly promoted Russian Premier League club reportedly viewing the Maccabi Netanya midfielder as a candidate to strengthen their engine room during the current transfer window. The interest surfaced in Russian media on Friday and was carried by two Israeli outlets, though it has not hardened into a formal approach.

Zaarura, 23, is a right-footed central midfielder from Shefar'am who came through Maccabi Haifa's academy before moving to Netanya in 2023. A loan spell at Ironi Tiberias preceded his breakthrough, and on his return he produced the most productive campaign of his career.
The report credits him with ten goals from 24 appearances in all competitions, a striking return for a player equally comfortable screening the back four.

His contract at the Netanya Stadium runs until June 2027, so Rodina — or anyone else — would have to agree a fee rather than wait for a free transfer. Transfermarkt lists his value at €350,000 as of June, a figure that looks modest against Russian top-flight budgets but hands Netanya a floor from which to negotiate. Any sale would still require the club's consent.

Rodina are an unusual suitor. Founded in 2015 around a Moscow youth academy and bankrolled by businessman Sergey Lomakin, they sealed a top-two finish in the Russian First League last season to reach the Premier League for the first time in their history, and are now recruiting players capable of surviving the step up in class.
For Zaarura, capped three times by Israel's Under-21 side, the calculation would set a bigger league and salary against leaving the Israeli Premier League just as his club form has peaked.
For now nothing is agreed. The interest remains a media report without club confirmation, and any deal would run through Maccabi Netanya's boardroom first.

title: Sharp signs off Summer League with 16 points as Kings edge Hornets
dek: The Tel Aviv-born guard hit four three-pointers and added three steals in Sacramento's 92–90 win over Charlotte, closing his first Summer League with his most rounded performance yet.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: עמנואל שארפ בלט עם 16 נקודות בניצחון סקרמנטו

body: Emanuel Sharp closed out his first NBA Summer League the way Sacramento would have scripted it, leading the scoring in a win. The Tel Aviv-born guard finished with 16 points, four three-pointers, three assists and three steals in 30 minutes on Friday in Las Vegas as the Kings held off the Charlotte Hornets 92–90 to close their fortnight in Nevada.

Sacramento built the platform early, taking the first quarter 31–19 and stretching the lead to 15. Charlotte clawed the deficit down to five by half-time, then later moved six points clear, in a contest that swung through eight changes of lead before the Kings regained control inside the final four minutes and protected a two-point edge to the buzzer.
For Sharp, the line mattered less for its size than its shape. He shot 5-of-12 from the field and 4-of-9 from distance, made his only free throw, and gave the ball away just once.

His Las Vegas appearances traced a familiar rookie arc in these pages: 23 points on scorching shooting against Brooklyn, then a laboured 4-of-13 evening against Boston. This closing performance sat neatly between the two — efficient without being hot, productive without monopolising the offence.

He had help. Jonathan Mogbo filled the sheet with 14 points, eight rebounds, four assists and three blocks, while Alex Karaban added 14 of his own. Charlotte's resistance ran through Hannes Steinbach, whose 22 points and 11 rebounds on 7-of-10 shooting kept the Hornets within a possession until the end.
The result carried no silverware — both sides were playing in the consolation bracket — and the win took Sacramento to 2–3 for the tournament while Charlotte finished 1–4.

For a second-round pick, though, standings are largely beside the point. Sharp leaves Las Vegas having led the Kings' scoring in the finale, and having attached steals and quiet turnover columns to almost every outing — the unglamorous habits that tend to decide whether a 45th selection earns a role.

The Israeli interest in that progress is direct. Sharp was born and raised in Tel Aviv, the son of Derrick Sharp, the long-serving Maccabi Tel Aviv guard and captain, and represented Israel at junior international level before his college career at Houston. Sacramento's decision to spend the 45th pick of last month's draft on him promised nothing beyond an audition — and on the evidence of the finale, perimeter shooting that travelled, hands that keep producing deflections, decisions that held up late in a tight game, that audition has done enough to continue into training camp.

The Kings closed their Summer League at 2–3 and the Hornets finished 1–4.

body: Barak Abramov chose Friday night television for his first extended response to the most violent week his business empire has known. Interviewed by Haim Etgar on Ulpan Shishi after grenades, arson attempts and suspected gunfire struck branches of his Japanika restaurant chain — nine of them in a single week, by his own count in a parallel Globes account of the broadcast — the Beitar Jerusalem owner insisted he had received no threats and offered a striking new claim about why his name keeps surfacing.

According to the Israeli report of the interview, Abramov said that beyond the underworld feud he insists he has no part in, he has fallen victim to a second dispute. "What is happening in the deal with Leumi Partners and what is happening in the media — I am the victim of a 'conflict', I fell between two people," he said. He identified those parties as the leadership of Keshet and Victor Vakrat, today chief executive of Leumi Partners and previously head of Keshet's business division. "The heads of Keshet did not like Victor leaving for Leumi Partners; apparently they waited for him around the corner, and who takes the fire — Japanika and Barak Abramov," he claimed. He offered no evidence for the allegation, which he delivered on Keshet 12's own Friday programme, and the report carries no response from Keshet, Vakrat or Leumi Partners.

The business backdrop, unlike the allegation, is independently established. Leumi Partners, Bank Leumi's investment arm, recently paid about 200 million shekels for 20 per cent of Abramov's Landora group, Japanika's parent, at a valuation of roughly one billion shekels — figures confirmed in both Ynet and Globes reporting. Ynet has quoted bank sources saying the firm would exit the partnership if an investigation established involvement with criminal elements, and that a planned stock-market flotation is expected to be postponed. "It is clear I got a phone call from them — they are my partners," Abramov said of the firm.

His denials were categorical. "I was not threatened, I received no threat," he said, adding: "There is no proof that I was, will be or am currently a partner of criminal elements." He turned the charge back on his interviewers, noting that Keshet itself had once been his partner in a venture: "So Keshet are also partners with criminals?" In the Globes account of the same broadcast, he acknowledged limited acquaintance with the Musli and Jarushi crime families while denying any friendship or business relationship, and said National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir's office had told him in a conference call with senior police officers that they know he has no business ties to the families; police, he said, asked for a list of all 46 branches in order to protect them.

None of that settles what police themselves suspect. Independent reporting in Walla describes an assessment that the attacks form part of a coordinated conflict between the Musli and Jarushi families, with roughly 15 grenades thrown across the Tel Aviv area within a week and concern that stolen military weaponry is in circulation. Abramov's own account of why Japanika became a target — sadness and bafflement in one breath, a media feud in the next — remains his characterisation, not an established finding, and the two explanations sit unresolved alongside each other.

For Israeli football the relevance is unchanged from ILSP's earlier reporting: the attacks concern Abramov's private businesses, and neither Beitar Jerusalem nor its supporters are implicated in the investigation. But the interview aired hours before Beitar's heavily policed meeting with Hapoel Tel Aviv in Netanya, with the club's owner already under security escort, and his public posture now matters commercially as well as personally. The next verifiable developments are concrete ones: any response from Keshet or Leumi Partners, decisions on the flotation, and where the police investigation into the attacks leads.

title: Police chief behind Maccabi Tel Aviv's Villa Park ban left with £57,800 payout
dek: Draft accounts show Craig Guildford received about 236,000 shekels as compensation for loss of office after resigning over the discredited ban on Israeli supporters, a payment the UK's shadow justice secretary called 'a disgrace'.

source.name: Sport1 / Maariv

body: Craig Guildford, the former chief constable of West Midlands Police who oversaw the recommendation to ban Maccabi Tel Aviv supporters from last November's Europa League fixture at Aston Villa, left office with £57,800 — roughly 236,000 shekels — according to the force's draft statement of accounts for 2025/26. The sum is recorded as compensation for loss of office.

The figure came to light this week when Nick Timothy, Britain's shadow justice secretary, published the accounts on X. Timothy called the payment "a disgrace" and "a reward for failure", adding that "under pressure from Islamists and antisemites, West Midlands Police lied to justify banning Israeli fans from Villa Park".

The episode behind the payout is well documented. Ahead of the Aston Villa v Maccabi Tel Aviv match on 6 November 2025, the force recommended to Birmingham's safety advisory group that away supporters be barred from Villa Park on safety grounds — a decision that triggered an international outcry and months of scrutiny.

An inspection by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary, led by chief inspector Sir Andy Cooke, later found that the force had made misleading statements about Maccabi fans and given inaccurate information to a parliamentary committee. It had also relied in part on material generated by artificial intelligence — including a reference to a fixture that never took place — and had failed to consult Birmingham's Jewish community adequately.

Guildford initially told MPs that artificial intelligence had not been used in compiling the force's report, before admitting the claim was incorrect and apologising. He retired on 16 January 2026, at the age of 52, after Downing Street and the home secretary said they had lost confidence in his leadership.

The West Midlands police and crime commissioner's office has defended the payment. It said Guildford was legally entitled to three months' pay in lieu of notice plus outstanding leave, that he received "no more than the bare minimum he was contractually entitled to", and that his immediate retirement was more cost-effective than having him serve out a notice period on his £220,000 annual salary.
For Israeli football, the disclosure reopens a wound eight months after the match itself. The Villa Park ban became emblematic of the hostility Israeli clubs have faced abroad since October 2023.

News that the officer who presided over the discredited decision left with a six-figure shekel-equivalent payment — and no further sanction — has landed in Israel, as the sharp reaction in British politics shows, as an unresolved accountability question rather than a closed file.

body: Maccabi Haifa are closing in on the most profitable piece of business in their recent history. Heorhiy Yermakov, the club's Ukrainian goalkeeper, is set to be sold to Metalist Kharkiv for a fee reported at around €3m, with Saturday morning reporting indicating a formal announcement is expected within 48 hours.
The sum remains reported rather than confirmed by either club, but Israeli coverage is already billing it as a record sale — roughly thirty times the €100,000 Haifa were said to have paid for him.

It is a remarkable arc for a goalkeeper whose story has always carried an Israeli thread. Yermakov, 24, was born in Kyiv to a Ukrainian Jewish family; his parents emigrated to Holon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A product of Shakhtar Donetsk's academy, he established himself at Oleksandriya, where Haifa spotted him early. The club secured his rights and loaned him back for the 2024-25 season, in which he was named the Ukrainian Premier League's goalkeeper of the year before finally arriving in Israel, where he made 32 appearances wearing the number 89 shirt.

One season, it turns out, was enough to multiply his value many times over. If the reported figure holds, the deal would extend a striking summer for Israeli clubs in the export market — Hapoel Jerusalem completed a record €1.6m sale of John Otomewo to Stade de Reims only this week — and hand Haifa a war chest at precisely the moment their squad rebuild demands one.
The succession plan is already in motion. Israeli reporting says Omri Glazer will sign as Yermakov's replacement, the final act of a pursuit that has run all summer.

As covered on Friday, Red Star Belgrade are said to be demanding around €250,000 before releasing the Israel international, who has reportedly agreed personal terms on a return to the club where he won the 2020-21 championship. Selling one goalkeeper for a reported €3m while paying a fraction of that to land his successor would, on paper, be the cleanest exchange of Haifa's window.
The morning's other item is more delicate. Manuel Benson's situation will be examined, the report says, as the winger works his way back from injury.

The Belgian, who joined permanently from Burnley on 1 February 2026 on a contract running to June 2027, has a long and documented history of Achilles tendon trouble from his Burnley years, and the Israeli report frames his current recovery in those terms. Transfermarkt's injury log, however, records his most recent absence as a hamstring strain dating from early May. Either way, Haifa must now decide what a fit Benson is worth to their season — and what an unfit one costs.

The rest of the briefing points to a club accelerating through pre-season. Andrija Novakovich, whose agreement was announced last week, is expected in Israel in the coming days for his medical and signing; Yarin Levy is in line for improved terms after Tisha B'Av, with a reported €2.5m release clause; and a training match against Hapoel Kfar Saba is scheduled for Tuesday.

Nothing is done until it is announced, and the fee, the timetable and the record framing all rest on Saturday's report. But with the Toto Cup opener against Hapoel Haifa looming at the end of the month, the shape of Haifa's summer is suddenly legible: one goalkeeper sold at an extraordinary profit, another coming home to replace him, and a €3m question already answered before the season has begun.

Update, 18 July: Maccabi Haifa and Metalist Kharkiv have now agreed terms on Yermakov's transfer, according to aligned reporting in Israel and Ukraine on Saturday evening. Neither club has made an official announcement, but accounts on both sides describe the deal as settled, with the goalkeeper expected to travel to Ukraine within the coming week to complete the move.

The fee continues to be reported at approximately €3 million, though Ukrainian reporting earlier this month placed the compromise closer to €3.2 million; no figure has been confirmed by either club. Personal terms were agreed in early July, and Haifa are reported to be lining up Omri Glazer as Yermakov's replacement.

Update, 19 July: agreement has reportedly now been reached on Yarin Levy's new contract, though nothing is yet signed — the formal announcement is being held back until after Tisha B'Av. Levy, returning after two seasons on loan at Beitar Jerusalem, is in line for a significant salary increase, and the latest account says the deal will carry no release clause covering the current or winter transfer windows, a shift from earlier reporting of a €2.5m clause.

The reported €3m is roughly thirty times the €100,000 Haifa were reported to have paid for Yermakov, whose rights the club secured from Oleksandriya before loaning him back for 2024-25, when he was named Ukrainian Premier League goalkeeper of the year; he made 32 appearances for Haifa.

title: Fifty years on: Montreal 1976, the black ribbon and Israel's first Olympic finalist
dek: The Games that opened on 17 July 1976 asked Israel's athletes simply to show up four years after Munich. Esther Roth-Shahamorov answered by racing into an Olympic final — and resetting what Israeli sport thought it was for.

source.name: ILSP Archive Desk
source.originalTitle: From the Archive
source.author: ILSP Sports Desk

verificationSources.label: Olympedia — Esther Shakhamorov-Roth, athlete results
Olympedia — 1976 Montreal Summer Olympics edition page
Wikipedia — Israel at the 1976 Summer Olympics
Wikipedia — Esther Roth-Shahamorov
Wikipedia — Munich massacre (Montreal 1976 commemoration)

body: Fifty years ago this weekend, on 17 July 1976, Queen Elizabeth II declared the Montreal Olympics open in front of a stadium that was still, in places, a building site. Among the delegations filing past the royal box was one whose flag carried something no other did: a black ribbon, tied on for the eleven Israeli team members murdered at the Munich Games four years earlier. Holding that flag aloft was a 24-year-old sprint hurdler from Tel Aviv, Esther Roth-Shahamorov, and no athlete in the stadium carried more of the story in her own body.

In Munich in 1972, Roth had been Israel's brightest track prospect. She reached the semi-finals of the 100 metres and qualified for the semi-finals of the 100 metres hurdles — and then never ran them. On 5 September, members of the Palestinian group Black September seized the Israeli quarters in the Olympic village; by the end of the failed rescue at Fürstenfeldbruck, eleven Israelis were dead. Among them was Amitzur Shapira, the coach who had guided Roth since her teens. Israel withdrew from the Games, and Roth went home with her career suspended mid-stride.

Montreal was therefore never going to be an ordinary Olympics for Israel. The delegation of 28 competitors — 26 men and two women, across ten sports — arrived at Games already diminished by a 26-nation boycott, most of it African, over New Zealand's rugby ties with apartheid South Africa. Ninety-two countries remained. For Israel, the temptation was to treat the fortnight as an act of witness: march, mourn, be seen to have returned. The black ribbon on the flag said exactly that.

Roth refused to let remembrance be the whole assignment. She had spent the intervening years proving the point in stages, winning sprint and hurdles gold at the 1974 Asian Games in Tehran, and she came to Canada in the form of her life. Her 12.93 seconds for the hurdles that year would stand as the Israeli record for the next quarter of a century.

In Montreal she moved through the rounds of the 100 metres hurdles and, in doing so, crossed a line no Israeli had crossed: she became the first athlete from the country, in any sport, to reach an Olympic final.

The final itself delivered a result that reads modestly and meant everything. Roth finished sixth in 13.04 seconds. No medal, no podium — but a placing among the eight fastest hurdlers on earth, achieved by an athlete whose previous Olympics had ended in a morgue's shadow rather than on a track.
Half a century later she remains Israel's only Olympic track finalist, a fact that measures both her quality and how steep the mountain has stayed.

Nor was she carrying the delegation alone. Weightlifter Eduard Weitz finished fifth in his class, at that point the best Olympic placing by any Israeli in any sport, and the footballers ground out three draws to reach the quarter-finals before Brazil ended their run. Quietly, in the most emotionally loaded fortnight Israeli sport had known, Montreal became its most successful Games to date.

That is the real argument of Montreal 1976: it is the moment Israeli Olympic sport stopped being defined solely by what had been done to it and started being defined by what it could do. The ribbon and the finish line coexisted on the same flag.

Roth's national record survived until Irina Lenskiy lowered it in 2002, and the idea she raced into being — that an Israeli athlete belongs in an Olympic final on merit, not on sympathy — outlasted even the record. Fifty years on, as another World Cup weekend fills the calendar, that July evening in Montreal remains the hinge on which a sporting culture turned.
facts: The Montreal Olympics opened on 17 July 1976, with Queen Elizabeth II declaring the Games open; 92 countries took part after a 26-nation boycott, most of it African, over New Zealand's rugby tour of apartheid South Africa.
Israel's flag entered the opening ceremony adorned with a black ribbon in memory of the eleven team members murdered at the 1972 Munich Games, and Esther Roth-Shahamorov was Israel's flag-bearer.
At Munich 1972, Roth reached the 100m semi-finals and qualified for the 100m hurdles semi-finals, but Israel withdrew after the massacre, in which her long-time coach Amitzur Shapira was killed.
In Montreal, Roth finished sixth in the 100m hurdles final in 13.04 seconds, becoming the first Israeli athlete in any sport to reach an Olympic final.
Her 1976 personal best of 12.93 seconds stood as the Israeli 100m hurdles record for 26 years, until Irina Lenskiy broke it in 2002.

Israel sent 28 competitors (26 men, two women) across ten sports to Montreal; weightlifter Eduard Weitz's fifth place was then Israel's best-ever Olympic result, and the football team reached the quarter-finals before losing to Brazil.

title: Israeli football has learned how to sell — now the fees have to become real
dek: A goalkeeper bought for a reported €100,000 heading out at a reported €3m, a confirmed €1.6m record in Jerusalem, a champion keeper coming home for small change: this summer's trading looks like strategy. Whether it is a model depends on what is confirmed — and repeated.

source.originalTitle: ILSP weekend column
source.author: ILSP Sports Desk

body: Somewhere in the paperwork between Kyiv, Holon and Kharkiv sits the number that defines Israeli football's summer. Heorhiy Yermakov, a goalkeeper whose rights Maccabi Haifa were reported to have bought for around €100,000, is expected to leave for Metalist Kharkiv at a reported €3m — a thirtyfold return on a single season's work, if the figure survives contact with an official announcement.

Four days earlier, Hapoel Jerusalem completed a club-record €1.6m sale of John Otomewo to Stade de Reims, a midfielder they found at a talent tournament in Nigeria barely a year ago. Israeli clubs have always sold players. This column is not sure they have ever traded quite like this.
The shape of the business is what has changed. The old Israeli export was reactive: a European club noticed a star, an offer arrived, the money was taken. This summer's dealing looks designed.

Haifa bought Yermakov's rights from Oleksandriya early and cheaply, loaned him straight back for a standout season in the Ukrainian top flight, and imported him with the value already compounding. Jerusalem put a Nigerian teenager through their youth side, gave him 21 senior appearances in a relegation fight, and sold him inside twelve months. Hapoel Petah Tikva, at the other end of the price scale, re-signed Franck Rivollier on a free with a two-season option — a proven forward acquired for nothing, his resale window still open.

Otomewo is the cleanest evidence, because his fee is the only headline number a club has actually put its name to. A supporter-owned side with modest commercial income turned a scouting trip, a youth-team place and one trusted season into the largest sale in its history — and the sale is credible precisely because the development was real. He was not warehoused and flipped; he was played, in the least forgiving position on a struggling team, until the projection became fact. That is what a develop-and-sell economy looks like when it works: the football and the finance confirming each other.
Yermakov is the bigger multiple and the softer number. Nothing has been announced by either club; the €3m, the 48-hour timetable and the record framing all rest on weekend reporting.

The same caution applies to Omri Glazer, whose compensation to Red Star Belgrade moved from a reported €250,000 to an estimated €300,000 within a day — a reminder that these are negotiations being narrated in real time, not accounts being filed. A responsible reading of this window keeps two ledgers: one for what clubs have confirmed, which is impressive, and one for what reporters expect, which is spectacular. They are not the same ledger.

Glazer's return shows the other half of the machine. At 30, with three Serbian titles and 23 caps for Israel, he is reportedly coming home for a fraction of the €1.5m fee attached to his departure in 2023, on wages Haifa can justify because the transfer outlay is trivial. Selling players near the top of their value curve and re-importing proven internationals on the descending side of it is exactly how sensible mid-sized leagues behave. The exchange Haifa are attempting — a reported €3m in for one goalkeeper, roughly a tenth of that out for his successor — would be, on paper, the tidiest single piece of business an Israeli club has done in years.

Mohammed Abu Fani supplies both the advert and the warning. The Israel midfielder moved to Red Star in June for a reported €1m, then played every minute of a 5-0 league opener in Belgrade — proof that Israeli-developed players now carry a price and a role at Champions League-chasing clubs.

But that €1m went to Ferencváros, not to anyone in Israel, because Haifa sold him in 2023 at an earlier point on the curve. Israeli football built the asset; Hungarian football banked the appreciation.

The corrective is already visible in the small print: Haifa are reported to have kept a sell-on percentage in the Yermakov deal, and did the same when Liam Hermesh left on a free for Graz. Clubs that once sold endings are learning to sell options.

There are harder objections than timing. Reported fees are not confirmed fees, and deals die late: Anan Khalaili had agreed terms and a concluded negotiation with one of Europe's biggest clubs, and the transfer still collapsed at the Italian registration stage. A summer's arithmetic can shrink considerably between the back pages and the bank. Until Kharkiv and Belgrade publish announcements, the honest description of Haifa's window is a plan, not a profit.

The second objection is the product itself. Jerusalem open the season without the holding midfielder they trusted through a relegation fight; Haifa, if the deal completes, without a goalkeeper who played 32 matches for them. A league that exports its best arguments for watching it is making a real sacrifice, and no sell-on clause refunds the supporter.

The answer every successful selling league has offered — Belgium, Austria, Croatia — is that the drain is survivable if the money is reinvested in the machine that generated it: the scouting routes, the academy minutes, the willingness to start teenagers. Spent on wages instead, it merely purchases a slower decline.

And one window is not a trend. Two record sales in a week can be a coincidence of two good players maturing at once. The test of a model is repetition: whether Israeli clubs are buying the next Yermakov this month, whether the route that found Otomewo in Nigeria is a programme or an anecdote, and whether next summer's fees arrive because European buyers now price Israeli development seriously rather than opportunistically.
So this column will resist the celebration and decline the cynicism. What happened this summer is neither accident nor arrival.

The structures — early rights purchases, loan-backs, sell-on clauses, cheap re-imports of proven internationals — are too deliberate to dismiss, and too new, and too dependent on unconfirmed numbers, to canonise. Israeli football has taught itself the grammar of a selling league. Whether it is fluent will be decided by two announcements it does not control, and by whether it can do all of this again when nobody is calling it a record.
facts: Hapoel Jerusalem announced a club-record €1.6m sale of John Otomewo to Stade de Reims after one season and 21 senior appearances; he joined their youth side in summer 2025 after being identified at a talent tournament in Nigeria.

Maccabi Haifa goalkeeper Heorhiy Yermakov is reported to be joining Metalist Kharkiv for around €3m — a fee that is reported, not club-confirmed — after Haifa reportedly paid about €100,000 for his rights from Oleksandriya and loaned him back for 2024-25; he made 32 appearances for Haifa.

Israeli reporting puts Maccabi Haifa's compensation to Red Star Belgrade for Omri Glazer at an estimated €300,000, up from a reported €250,000 demand a day earlier; Glazer, 30, left Israel for a reported €1.5m in 2023 and has won three Serbian titles.

Red Star Belgrade paid Ferencváros a reported €1m, with up to €300,000 in bonuses, for Israel midfielder Mohammed Abu Fani in June 2026; he played the full 90 minutes of their 5-0 SuperLiga opener on 17 July.
Hapoel Petah Tikva re-signed French forward Franck Rivollier on a free transfer on a one-year deal with a two-season option.
Anan Khalaili's proposed transfer from Union Saint-Gilloise to Inter collapsed at the Italian sporting-fitness registration stage despite agreed personal terms.
Maccabi Haifa are reported to retain sell-on percentages on both the Yermakov deal and Liam Hermesh's free transfer to Grazer AK.

body: Bnei Sakhnin have completed the signing of Romanian goalkeeper Raul Bălbărău, the club announced on Saturday, adding a fresh contender for the number-one shirt ahead of the 2026/27 Israeli Premier League season. The 25-year-old arrives as a free agent after his contract at top-flight side Petrolul Ploiești expired this summer. He has agreed a one-year deal that carries a club option for two further seasons.

Bălbărău, who stands 1.89 metres and was born in Galați, spent the past two and a half years at Petrolul after joining in early 2024, making 47 appearances in all competitions and keeping 14 clean sheets. Last season he played 30 matches, conceding 36 goals with seven shut-outs, as the Ploiești club finished 12th in Romania's top division and preserved their status by a margin of three points.

His route to the Romanian top flight was not a conventional one. He won the Liga III title with the historic Steaua București club in 2020/21, then moved to Debrecen in Hungary, where league opportunities never came. A loan spell at Noah in Armenia gave him regular senior football instead.

He has been capped once at under-21 level for Romania, in 2022, and is valued at around half a million euros. One report noted that he also holds Moldovan citizenship, a detail matched by his transfer-registry record.

The goalkeeper becomes the sixth signing of Sakhnin's busy summer window, following Iyad Abu Abid, Modestus Vorobjovas, Niv Livnat, Norberto Carlos and Sana Gomes, and the fourth foreign player recruited for the new campaign. He is expected to link up with a squad currently at a pre-season training camp in Hungary under head coach Yossi Abukasis, who took charge of the club in February.

The arrival immediately raises questions about the standing of Mohammed Abu Nil, the 24-year-old who has been Sakhnin's first-choice goalkeeper in recent seasons. According to one account, the incumbent's representatives were surprised by the move, having understood that he had been assured of the starting role. How that competition is resolved may become one of the more delicate management tasks of Abukasis's first full pre-season in charge.

For a club that finished last season in mid-table and is aiming higher, the logic of the signing is straightforward: proven top-flight minutes in a comparable European league, at no transfer fee, on terms that protect the club if the move succeeds. The option structure means Sakhnin can retain Bălbărău until 2029 if he establishes himself, while committing to only a single season up front.

The recruitment drive is not finished. The club is still reported to be pursuing a striker and an additional winger before the window closes, suggesting the squad that opens the campaign may yet look different again from the one currently working in Hungary.

Update, 19 July: reporting the following morning added a sharper edge to the goalkeeping question. Abu Nil is said to have learned of Bălbărău's signing through the media rather than from the club, with those close to him expressing surprise at the decision.
Abu Nil came up through Sakhnin's own system, while the push for a new goalkeeper is reported to have come from coach Yossi Abukasis. Bălbărău is expected to join the squad's training camp shortly.

body: Four clubs from across Europe are reportedly tracking Maccabi Tel Aviv winger Hélio Varela, according to Israeli reports published on Saturday. Samsunspor of Turkey, Qarabağ of Azerbaijan, Red Star Belgrade of Serbia and Hungarian champions Ferencváros are the sides named, with the interest attributed to coverage that surfaced in Turkey alongside Cape Verdean media.

No formal bid has been reported. Varela's contract at Bloomfield Stadium runs until 30 June 2028, and Hebrew-language accounts note that any move this summer would hinge entirely on Maccabi Tel Aviv's financial demands and its willingness to sell a player it tied down on a long-term deal less than a year ago.

The 24-year-old was born in Almada, Portugal, and is a Cape Verde international with 23 caps. He arrived in Israel on 4 September 2025 from Belgian side Gent, for a fee reported at around €1.5 million, following a difficult single season in Belgium.
Transfermarkt now values him at €2.5 million, double the figure the site recorded when he signed.
His debut Israeli campaign explains the attention. Varela recorded three goals and two assists in Ligat ha'Al from the left flank and collected a domestic cup winners' medal.
He then raised his profile further at the 2026 World Cup, where he is reported to have scored his first international goal in three appearances during Cape Verde's historic maiden finals.

The appeal differs among the reported suitors. Qarabağ, Red Star and Ferencváros are serial domestic champions able to offer European group-stage football, while the Israeli assessment holds that Samsunspor — without European competition this season and already well stocked with left-sided wingers — may be the least natural fit for the player's ambitions.

For Maccabi, losing Varela would strip out one of the squad's few natural left wingers just as European qualification rounds approach. But with two years still to run on his contract, the club holds every card, and unless one of the four turns reported admiration into an offer that meets Tel Aviv's valuation, this remains interest — nothing more.

body: A release clause of just €100,000 has turned Maccabi Netanya's brightest academy product into the talk of Israeli football. Yarin Abuhatzira, a 16-year-old forward already training with the senior squad, was described on a national radio programme as the best player in the country for his age. With clubs said to be starting to ask about him, Netanya are scrambling to tear up the clause before somebody simply pays it.

"There is a huge player at Maccabi Netanya — they say he is the best in the country for his age," pundit Moshe Primo told listeners during the discussion, citing the esteem in which figures such as Benny Lam and Israel youth coach Ofir Haim are said to hold the teenager.

Former international Michael Zandberg argued that €100,000 is disproportionately low for a prospect of this calibre. Ofir Saar summed up the mood on the coast: "There is pressure around Maccabi Netanya, they are trying to close a new contract with him."

The hype has a paper trail. Abuhatzira, born in 2010 and the son of Shimon Abuhatzira — the 2008-09 league top scorer who won the title with Ironi Kiryat Shmona in 2011-12 and earned three Israel caps — spent last season playing a year above his age group and still finished with 29 goals in all competitions.
An Israel youth international, he signed a three-year academy contract in May 2025 and was promoted into the first-team setup before his 16th birthday.

Separate Israeli reporting corroborates the contract picture: his current deal runs for two more years and carries a buy-out worth only a few hundred thousand shekels, in line with the €100,000 figure. Chairman Gil Lev has accelerated talks on a new senior contract with improved terms, and the player's father and his agent, Nir Amir, recently visited Netanya's training camp in Poland to push the negotiations along. The proposed deal would extend his stay and remove the clause altogether.

Netanya's strongest card may be the one no bigger club can play: first-team football at 16. No named suitor has yet lodged a bid, and the expectation on all sides is that a new agreement will be signed. Until the paperwork is done, though, one of Israeli football's most coveted teenagers can be had for the price of a mid-table squad player's annual wage.

body: Maccabi Haifa have completed the permanent sale of Show to Kocaelispor, the departure officially announced on Saturday evening and bringing a quietly unsuccessful chapter on the Carmel to a tidy conclusion. The Turkish top-flight club, where the Angolan midfielder spent last season on loan, will pay 500,000 euros for a player who made just 21 league appearances in green.

The 27-year-old defensive midfielder — Manuel Luís da Silva Cafumana, known throughout his career simply as Show — is set to sign a three-year contract worth a reported 500,000 euros per season. The fee itself will be paid in instalments, though accounts of the schedule differ: reporting in Israel describes payments spread across two years, while Turkish coverage of the deal refers to three instalments instead.

Kocaelispor's loan arrangement included a purchase option, and the club has now moved to exercise it. Show is expected to join pre-season training at Topuk Yaylası once the final formalities are completed.

Show arrived in Haifa in August 2023 from Ludogorets Razgrad with a pedigree that promised more than he ultimately delivered. A product of Primeiro de Agosto in Luanda, he had earned a move to Lille as a 20-year-old in 2019, gathered experience on loan at B-SAD and Boavista in Portugal, and then established himself over two seasons in Bulgaria.

At Maccabi Haifa, though, he never commanded a regular place. He finished his single active season with 32 appearances in all competitions and a reputation as one of the squad's more expensive misfits.
What followed was a loan odyssey. Haifa first sent him to FC Dallas, where he made 13 appearances in Major League Soccer, before Kocaelispor took him for the 2025-26 campaign.

There, finally, the fit worked. Show made 30 appearances for the side from İzmit, and Turkish reports describe him as one of the players head coach Selçuk İnan trusted most, as well as a favourite with the club's supporters — the kind of season that made a permanent deal feel inevitable.

For Maccabi Haifa, the sale is best read as housekeeping with a modest return. Show's contract ran until 2027 and his market valuation stood at roughly 1.5 million euros this spring, so the fee falls short of what the club once hoped the midfielder might be worth.
Still, it removes a substantial foreign-player salary from the books, frees a slot in the squad, and converts an asset who was never going to play for the club again into cash.

For the player, the move offers stability in a league where he has already proved himself. Show remains a regular for Angola, with more than 50 senior caps and an appearance at the Africa Cup of Nations, and a settled club home in the Turkish top flight gives him a platform to protect that international standing into his late twenties.

body: Abdoulaye Seck is reportedly on the point of joining Al-Faisaly, with accounts in Saudi Arabia picked up by Israeli outlets on Saturday indicating that the 34-year-old centre-back has travelled to the Gulf and was expected to put his signature to a contract with the newly promoted Saudi Pro League club later in the day. Seck left Maccabi Haifa this summer when his contract expired after four seasons, so the move would involve no transfer fee.

Nothing has yet been formally announced by the club or the player, and the reports stop short of describing a completed deal: Seck is said to have arrived to sign rather than to have signed. The one official trace so far is a post from the Saudi Pro League's account on X stating that the defender would sign on Saturday. Contract length and salary have not been reported.

That post carried its own sting for supporters in Israel. In introducing the incoming defender, the league's announcement made no mention of Maccabi Haifa or of any part of his career in Israeli football — an omission noted pointedly in Israeli coverage, given that his years at Haifa were the most decorated of his club career.

Seck arrived in Israel from Royal Antwerp in the summer of 2022 and became a cornerstone of the side that won the 2022/23 championship, adding the Toto Cup and the Super Cup and earning recognition as the league's best foreign player that season. He made more than 140 appearances in all competitions for the club, scoring 14 goals — none more famous than his double against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League group stage in October 2022.

Al-Faisaly return to the Saudi top flight after winning promotion, and Seck would reportedly become their second overseas signing of the window following the arrival of forward Alexander Mendy from French football. For a club preparing for life back in the elite, a physically imposing defender with continental experience represents a low-cost, high-experience addition.

For Seck himself, the move would extend a late-career peak. A winner of the Africa Cup of Nations with Senegal in 2021, he has won 26 caps and was named in his country's squad for this summer's World Cup in North America. At 34, a first contract in the Gulf would open a fresh chapter — even if, on the evidence of its first announcement, his new league is in no hurry to dwell on where the previous one was written.

body: Maccabi Haifa announced on Saturday evening that Brazilian defender Wenderson Tsunami has signed for the club, adding an experienced and versatile option to a back line being rebuilt ahead of the 2026/27 campaign. The 30-year-old arrives as a free agent after his contract at Turkish second-tier side Igdir expired at the end of last season; no contract length was disclosed at the time.

There was a shade of nuance around the deal's status. Haifa's own statement said plainly that Tsunami had signed, while parallel reporting described him as having merely agreed personal terms, due to land in Israel on Saturday evening with medical checks still to follow. Either way, the club had made the move public, saying it believed his experience and his ability to cover several positions across the defence would serve the team in the competitions ahead.

Born Wenderson de Freitas Soares on 4 January 1996, the 1.89-metre defender is a left-back by trade with a strong left foot, though in recent seasons he has been used increasingly at centre-half, and he played defensive midfield earlier in his career. That flexibility is precisely what Haifa highlighted in announcing the signing.
He learned the game in Brazil's lower divisions, passing through Remo, Cuiaba and Botafogo-PB among others, and lifted the Copa Verde with Cuiaba in 2019.

The defining chapter of his career came in Bulgaria. Tsunami joined Levski Sofia in January 2022 and went on to make 112 appearances over four years, winning the Bulgarian Cup in his first half-season and eventually wearing the captain's armband at one of the country's biggest clubs.

This past January he moved on to Igdir in the Turkish second division, where he became a regular — accounts of his appearance tally there sit in the mid-teens — before his short-term deal ran its course over the summer.

Israeli supporters may already have seen him up close. During his Levski years he faced Hapoel Be'er Sheva in European qualification, playing the full goalless first leg before an injury kept him out of the return. Now he crosses to the other side of that divide, joining an Israeli club with continental ambitions of its own.

For Haifa, the timing is pointed. The club open their formal season next Saturday with a Toto Cup derby against Hapoel Haifa, and the coaching staff have been eager to add defensive depth before the competitive fixtures pile up. A left-sided defender who can play two, arguably three, positions — and who has captained a club through title races and European nights — gives them cover in exactly the areas where last season's squad looked thin.

Update, 19 July: the deal is now fully done. Tsunami passed his medical on Sunday and formally signed a two-year contract with Maccabi Haifa, settling the nuance around Saturday's announcement; no option year or shirt number was disclosed.

"I'm excited to join Maccabi Haifa," the defender said. "I've heard a lot about this club and the power of the green fans, and I'm already looking forward to taking the field and helping the team achieve its goals."
Professional director Lior Refaelov called him "an experienced, versatile and quality player," adding that the captaincy at his previous club shows "his character and responsibility."

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv's patience with Iffe Lundberg is close to exhausted. After a full week without a single roster move, Israeli reporting on Saturday evening said the club has presented the Danish guard with an improved offer to extend his stay, expects his decision within days, and has privately begun preparing for the possibility that the answer never comes.

The sharpest line in the report belongs to an unnamed Maccabi official: "If in another week or more we are still without him, we'll need to compromise on a different player — the European options have narrowed significantly. We need an answer from him in the coming days." A second official is quoted saying the situation "cannot continue much longer." Both remarks are attributed to anonymous club figures, not to named executives, and the club has made no on-record statement.

Lundberg's side has its own explanation for the delay. According to the report, his representatives say several clubs have expressed interest, which has slowed his decision. The 31-year-old joined Maccabi in November 2025 after leaving Partizan Belgrade, and his renewal has been a live issue for weeks: in Friday's podcast interview, sponsor Arik Shtilman claimed the drawn-out talks were connected to a trimmed budget after the Yam Madar signing — an assertion that remains his alone.

On Lonnie Walker IV, the mood has shifted since the club sweated through his NBA release window earlier this month. The report says Maccabi expect his answer in the coming days and that the longer his silence lasts, the stronger the assessment he will stay in yellow next season — though officials stress they will not stand in his way if an attractive NBA offer materialises. Club records show Walker signed a two-year deal in July 2025 that included NBA exit clauses for both 2025 and 2026.

The wider squad picture explains the urgency. Since the offseason began, Maccabi's only additions are Madar and Bonzie Colson, while Tamir Blatt, Zach Hankins and Marcio Santos have departed. The frontcourt is the most pressing gap: sporting director Claudio Coldebella has been scouting NBA Summer League options — a route the club had hoped to avoid in favour of experienced European signings — with one official quoted: "We need two big men, and at least one must arrive soon."

What is established, then, is narrow but real: an improved offer to Lundberg with a self-imposed deadline measured in days, a Walker file trending towards continuity, and a centre rotation still to be built as training camp approaches. Everything beyond that — including who blinks first — rests on negotiations that Maccabi's own officials describe as running out of road.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv backer's sponsorship of referees' body ignites integrity row
dek: A three-season sponsorship of the Israeli referees' association by Micky Koppel's company — a long-time Maccabi Tel Aviv sponsor whose owner is a self-declared devoted fan of the club — has drawn fan criticism, forcing the association to defend the deal as non-exclusive and precedented.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: החסות של מיקי קופל באיגוד השופטים עוררה סערה
source.author: ONE editorial team

verificationSources.label: Maccabi Tel Aviv official — Koppel Group extends club sponsorship (2021)

Koppel's public response to the sponsorship row (19 Jul)

body: A new commercial sponsorship of the Israeli referees' association has provoked a heated debate about the boundaries between club interests and match officiating, after it emerged that the backer is a businessman long and publicly identified with Maccabi Tel Aviv. The deal, announced on Friday evening, places the logo of Start Koppel Group Ltd on the official shorts worn by referees in the Premier League and the men's National League.

The agreement is structured as a secondary sponsorship running for three seasons. It is worth 375,000 shekels in 2026/27 and 425,000 shekels in 2027/28, with an optional extension at 475,000 shekels for 2028/29.

Beyond the shirt — or rather shorts — placement, the package includes LED advertising at State Cup semi-finals and finals and at home matches of the national team, eleven match tickets, joint content promotions and professional lectures delivered by top-flight referees.

The controversy centres on the identity of the sponsor. Micky Koppel, founder and owner of the Koppel Group, is a self-declared lifelong Maccabi Tel Aviv supporter, and his company has sponsored the club for well over a decade, with its logo carried on the shorts of Maccabi's first and youth teams.

That his brand will now also appear on the shorts of the officials who referee Maccabi's matches struck many supporters of rival clubs as, at minimum, an unfortunate optic. Criticism surfaced quickly on social media, where the announcement triggered sharp verbal exchanges between Koppel himself and football fans questioning the propriety of the arrangement. No club or official body has been reported as lodging a formal objection.

The referees' association, chaired by Giora Anbar, together with the Israel Football Association, moved to defend the deal. In a clarification addressing exclusivity and conflict of interest, the bodies stressed that the company holds no exclusivity, that its parallel sponsorship of Maccabi Tel Aviv imposes no limitation whatsoever, and that Israeli football has long accommodated sponsors backing multiple institutions at once, citing Fattal Hotels, Disenhaus and the Blue energy-drink brand as precedents.

The episode lands at a sensitive moment for Israeli officiating. Anbar has previously written to federation leadership warning of a deteriorating public discourse towards referees, and any perception — however contested — that match officials carry the colours of one club's benefactor is likely to keep the governance question alive as the new season approaches.

Update, 19 July: Koppel has now responded publicly at length, saying he regards the connection between his company and football as "natural, positive and blessed" and that the group has invested in Israeli football "out of genuine love for the sport" for nearly two decades. He denied any conflict of interest, describing the referees' deal as a legitimate commercial collaboration, and claimed much of the online backlash stems from "sophisticated bot operations" manufacturing artificial outrage.
While acknowledging he has supported Maccabi Tel Aviv since childhood, he noted his company advertises at all stadiums, in all leagues and alongside all clubs.
facts: Start Koppel Group Ltd signed a secondary sponsorship with the Israeli referees' association covering three seasons: NIS 375,000 (2026/27), NIS 425,000 (2027/28) and an optional NIS 475,000 (2028/29).
The company's logo will appear on official referee shorts in the Premier League and the men's National League.
The package includes LED signage at cup semi-finals and finals and national-team home matches, 11 tickets, joint content promotions and lectures by top-flight referees.
Micky Koppel is a publicly identified, lifelong Maccabi Tel Aviv supporter whose company has sponsored the club since around 2009, with its logo on Maccabi's kit shorts.
The announcement sparked sharp social-media exchanges between Koppel and football fans; no formal objection by a club or official body was reported.
The referees' association and the IFA stated the deal involves no exclusivity and no limitation, citing multi-body sponsors Fattal Hotels, Disenhaus and Blue as precedents.

On 19 July Micky Koppel publicly defended the referees' sponsorship, denying any conflict of interest and attributing much of the social-media backlash to coordinated bot activity — a claim that remains his characterisation.

title: Chelsea agree £117m Morgan Rogers deal to make him Britain's costliest player
dek: Aston Villa have accepted a bid worth £117m for the England forward, per David Ornstein of The Athletic, with a medical set for Monday and a six-year contract to 2032 awaiting signature.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: שוברת את השוק: צ'לסי סיכמה על רכישת רוג'רס

body: Chelsea have reached a verbal agreement with Aston Villa to sign Morgan Rogers for £117m, according to David Ornstein of The Athletic, who broke the story on Friday evening. If completed at that figure, the transfer would make the 23-year-old the most expensive British footballer in history — a striking outcome for a player Villa refused all summer to describe as available.

It is worth being precise about what has and has not been done. Per British reporting, Villa have accepted Chelsea's bid and the clubs hold a verbal agreement; Rogers is in line for a six-year contract running to 2032, with an option for a further twelve months, and a medical has been pencilled in for Monday.
Neither club has announced anything. No paperwork has been signed, and the fee, contract and timetable all remain reported rather than official.

The money still demands attention. At £117m, Rogers would edge £1m past Elliot Anderson's £116m move to Manchester City as the record fee for a British player, while sitting below the outright British transfer record — the £125m Liverpool paid Newcastle for Alexander Isak in the summer of 2025.
Villa had briefed that only a British-record £130m would open negotiations at all, so the final figure represents a modest concession from a position of genuine strength.

Arsenal are the losers in this race. Both London clubs pursued Rogers, but the decisive intervention is said to have come from Chelsea's newly appointed head coach Xabi Alonso, with one account stating that Rogers 'made it clear he wanted Chelsea after speaking to Xabi Alonso'.
A reunion with his close friend Cole Palmer at Stamford Bridge did the rest.

Villa's hand was strong for a reason. Rogers is contracted until June 2031 and cost them a fraction of this fee when he arrived from Middlesbrough in February 2024 — a deal from which his boyhood development club retain a 20 per cent sell-on clause, meaning a meaningful slice of the £117m will flow down to Teesside.
Rogers, who has spent this summer in England's World Cup squad, arrives as an attacking midfielder or wide forward entering his peak years, with 18 senior caps already behind him.

What remains is the unglamorous part: the Monday medical, the signatures and the announcement. Until those land, this is an agreement in principle — but one that British football's market will feel for years.

At £117m the fee would surpass Elliot Anderson's £116m move to Manchester City as the record for a British player.
The outright British transfer record remains the £125m Liverpool paid Newcastle for Alexander Isak in summer 2025.
Villa had demanded a British-record £130m and insisted Rogers, contracted until June 2031, was not for sale.
Middlesbrough retain a 20 per cent sell-on clause from Rogers' February 2024 move to Villa.
Rogers, 23, chose Chelsea over Arsenal after speaking with new head coach Xabi Alonso, and is part of England's 2026 World Cup squad.

body: Assaf Tzur saved three penalties in a 3–1 shootout as Hapoel Tel Aviv reached the Toto Cup semi-finals, after Daniel Dappa's stoppage-time equaliser denied Beitar Jerusalem a 2–1 win that had looked settled. Shon Weissman's 76th-minute penalty, scored on his Beitar debut, had put the Jerusalem side back in front following first-half goals from Chico and Johnbosco Kalu.
But the night in Netanya ended with the red half of Hapoel celebrating, and Almog Cohen's first match as Beitar head coach finishing in the cruellest way available.

The evening began at temperature. Beitar opened with the possession-and-press football their new coach had promised, and flares were lit in their end inside six minutes despite the week's warnings. Doron Leidner was booked in the eighth minute for scything down Omer Atzili, and Nana Antwi and Boris Enow followed him into the book for fouls on the same flank.
Elyaniv Barda responded by withdrawing Leidner altogether on 27 minutes, sending on 20-year-old Ofer Gelbard in his place — a change that would go on to define the result.

Hapoel struck first against that early pattern. On 19 minutes Stav Turiel measured a long pass to the right, Emmanuel Boateng cushioned a header back across goal, and Chico rose to nod in. The reply took four minutes: Ziv Ben Shimol slid a fine pass into Kalu, whose finish carried more placement than power but beat Tzur all the same.
Kalu might have had two more before the half-hour, shooting wide from a ball over the top and then, after Marcus Coco lost possession, tamely at Tzur.

Beitar were the better side for most of the half, and Tzur kept his team in the contest. Daniel Worko, one of two debutants in Cohen's starting eleven alongside Eugene Ansah, drove a shot from inside the area that the goalkeeper turned behind. Tzur then clawed Atzili's curling free-kick out of the angle and, three minutes before the interval, flew to tip Ansah's first-time strike from Antwi's low cross around the post.
Hapoel's sharpest response of the half came from Turiel, whose shot after Andrian Kraev's pass smacked the outside netting. It was 1–1 at the break, and honestly so.

Atzili, on carefully managed minutes as he builds fitness, stayed inside at half-time with Timothy Muzie taking his place, and the contest lost some edge as substitutions multiplied. Turiel nearly put Hapoel ahead from a tight angle in the 66th minute, but Cohen's triple change on 58 proved the sharper intervention: among the three arrivals was Weissman, back in Israeli football after seven years abroad, on for Ansah for his first appearance in yellow and black.

The winner came from the game's youngest fault line. Muzie ran at Gelbard in the 74th minute and was brought down inside the area, and referee Snir Levi pointed to the spot. Weissman waited, then placed the penalty precisely inside the post — a first Beitar goal, on debut, at the first invitation.

Hapoel lost composure more than shape in the aftermath. Daniel Dappa and Lucas Falcão were booked for dissent within five minutes of each other, and Gelbard was withdrawn moments after conceding the kick.

With no extra time in the competition — a draw after 90 minutes goes straight to penalties — Barda's side committed bodies forward through roughly eight added minutes, and the pressure told. In the sixth of them, substitute Daniel Dappa forced the ball home for 2–2, silencing a Beitar end that had begun celebrating a winning start to the new era.
Yarden Shua, passed fit after the virus that had put his place in doubt, had come on and taken the captain's armband; now he watched the tie head to the one lottery no captain controls.

The shootout belonged entirely to Assaf Tzur. The goalkeeper, already Hapoel's best player across the 90 minutes, saved three of Beitar's four penalties as the shootout finished 3–1, completing a personal performance that Israeli social media spent the evening comparing to the great goalkeeping nights.

The neutral staging came with the security operation announced a day earlier, and police reported five arrests around the ground before kick-off; no attendance figure was published on the night. It is Hapoel Tel Aviv who advance to the semi-finals, and both clubs now turn to Europe: Beitar open their Conference League qualifier against AEK Larnaca on Thursday, while Hapoel begin their continental programme against Ludogorets.

The reactions afterwards fit the finish. Almog Cohen, disappointed that a promising first match in charge slipped away at the end, confirmed his faith will continue to come first alongside the job: "I will not compromise Shabbat — it is more important than anything," he said in post-match remarks.

Weissman described the occasion as "an intensity I had not seen" and said he could not wait to play in front of the club's crowd again. Elyaniv Barda was strikingly frank for a coach whose side went through: "Beitar were better than us," he admitted, while welcoming Dappa's late goal as a sign of the character his squad will need this season.

title: Belaga makes history with a triple-double as Israel U20s rout Latvia 96–74
dek: A 16-point, 12-assist, 10-rebound night from the captain and a 26–9 second quarter carried Israel into the ninth-place game against Lithuania at the FIBA U20 EuroBasket.

source.name: Sport 5
