body: Israel's under-20 men delivered the most emphatic performance of their classification campaign, beating Latvia 96–74 in the 9–12 classification round of the FIBA U20 EuroBasket at Arena Stožice II in Ljubljana. One night after a win over Italy had removed the threat of relegation, this result guaranteed a finish of ninth or tenth and set up a meeting with Lithuania in the ninth-place game that closes Israel's tournament.

The contest was effectively settled in the second quarter. Israel led 27–20 after ten minutes, then held Latvia to nine points in the second period while scoring 26 of its own, a stretch that included an 18–0 run recorded on the official game tracker. The 53–29 half-time score turned the second half into an exercise in game management; Latvia won the third quarter 26–22, but Israel's lead, which peaked at 29 points, was never seriously threatened.

The headline belonged to Rany Belaga. Israel's captain finished with 16 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds, a triple-double reported in Israel as the first ever recorded by an Israeli at this championship and only the eighth in the event's history.

Belaga had carried a heavy scoring load in the defeat by Greece. Here, his value lay in distribution — he repeatedly found shooters and cutters while still finishing as the game's leading figure on the official efficiency board.

His passing had willing targets. Tamir Gold was the game's top scorer with 25 points, doing most of his damage inside the arc, while Oren Sahar added 14 and Yonatan Keller nine as the rotation spread the rest of the total.

That balance answered a question that had followed the team since the Greece defeat, when two players had supplied almost three-fifths of the offence. This time the scoring arrived from every position group.

The official shooting comparison tells the story plainly: Israel converted 55 percent of its field-goal attempts against Latvia's 39 percent, and held its opponent to just 20 percent from three-point range. Arturs Ozols topped Latvia's side of the leader board, but no visiting player could alter a game that featured only three lead changes, played before a crowd of 160 with Fernando Calatrava, Marius Ciulin and Romana Stojanović officiating.

The stage arithmetic is now settled. Israel's round-of-16 defeat by Greece diverted the team into the 9–16 classification bracket, Thursday's 84–59 win over Italy secured Division A status for 2027, and this victory fixes the final range at ninth or tenth. Lithuania, 100–84 winners over Poland in the other 9–12 classification game, provide the last assignment of the tournament.

Whatever happens in that final game, the week's trajectory is clear. A campaign that risked being defined by one poor knockout night against Greece has instead closed with consecutive wins by 25 and 22 points, a place preserved among Europe's top division for the next age group, and a piece of individual history for its captain. Finishing ninth would make the recovery complete.

title: Pogačar dances to a fourth Tour stage win at Le Markstein as lead stretches to 4:30
dek: The yellow jersey attacked 1.5km below the Col du Haag summit and soloed home on the 155.3km Vosges stage from Mulhouse, extending his overall lead to 4:30 ahead of Sunday's summit finish at the Plateau de Solaison.

body: Tadej Pogačar danced away from the Tour de France once again on Saturday, winning stage 14 into Le Markstein Fellering for his fourth stage victory of this year's race. On the 155.3km mountain stage from Mulhouse through the Vosges, the Slovenian attacked roughly 1.5km below the summit of the Col du Haag, and within moments the race for yellow was effectively over for another day.

Nobody could follow. Pogačar crested the climb alone and powered across the plateau to the line in a winning time of 4:00:07, with his UAE Team Emirates-XRG teammate Isaac del Toro leading home the chase at 38 seconds. French teenager Paul Seixas of Decathlon CMA CGM took third at the same gap, while Remco Evenepoel, Florian Lipowitz and Juan Ayuso rolled in 50 seconds down.

The victory extended the general classification lead Pogačar has been building since his summit win on stage 10, when his advantage stood at 3:36. It is now 4:30 over Jonas Vingegaard of Visma-Lease a Bike, with Evenepoel of Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe third overall at 5:04. With the yellow jersey also topping the mountains classification, his rivals increasingly appear to be racing for second.

Seixas was the day's other winner. Third on the stage lifted the 19-year-old to fourth overall at 5:19 and into the white jersey of best young rider, which he took from Ayuso by a mere three seconds, with Del Toro a further 28 seconds back in that contest.

In the points classification, the sprinters' battle that has simmered since Stian Wærenskjold's record-breaking sprint win on stage 11 continues: Mads Pedersen leads on 397 points from Jasper Philipsen on 361, with Biniam Girmay third on 347.

There is no respite. Sunday's stage 15 takes the race 183.9km from Champagnole to another summit finish at the Plateau de Solaison, where Vingegaard and Evenepoel must find something — anything — to disturb a champion in full flight.

title: England win a ten-goal epic 6-4 as Saka hat-trick claims World Cup bronze
dek: Bukayo Saka's hat-trick and a stoppage-time Jude Bellingham goal crowned one of the wildest matches in World Cup history in Miami Gardens, while Kylian Mbappé's brace carried him past Lionel Messi as the tournament's all-time record scorer.

source.name: ONE

body: England took World Cup bronze in a match that will be replayed for years, beating France 6-4 in Saturday's third-place playoff at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens. Bukayo Saka completed a hat-trick from the penalty spot in the 87th minute, and Jude Bellingham added a sixth deep into stoppage time, closing out a game France had twice threatened to turn into one of the great World Cup comebacks after trailing 4-0 at half-time.

The first half belonged entirely to England. Declan Rice put them ahead in the third minute, Ezri Konsa headed in a second from a corner in the 18th, and Saka struck twice more before the break — in the 37th minute and again in first-half stoppage time.
At 4-0, British and American coverage described near-total English control, while the French press turned on a defence it judged to be in disarray.

France made four changes at the interval and very nearly rewrote the story. Kylian Mbappé converted from Michael Olise's pass within three minutes of the restart, and Bradley Barcola made it 4-2 in the 54th. When Mbappé struck again in the 66th minute, the deficit was down to a single goal with more than twenty minutes still to play.

The finish was chaos at both ends. Saka restored some breathing room from the spot in the 87th minute, only for Ousmane Dembélé to pull France back to 5-4 in the sixth minute of stoppage time. Bellingham settled the ten-goal epic two minutes later.

Mbappé's brace rewrote the tournament's history books in the process. His ninth and tenth goals of this World Cup put the Golden Boot beyond realistic reach, and the second of the pair — his 22nd World Cup goal overall — took him past Lionel Messi's all-time record of 21.
Messi, on eight for the tournament, now faces Spain with Argentina in Sunday's final in East Rutherford knowing the career scoring record changed hands on the eve of his biggest night.

For England, the win offered a measure of consolation after the semi-final defeat in Atlanta, where Argentina overturned their lead with two goals in the closing minutes. Thomas Tuchel's side produced their most fluent attacking display of the tournament, and in Saka — a reported fitness doubt in the build-up — they had the game's outstanding performer, his hat-trick bookending an evening in which England scored six and needed every one of them.

The result gives England their first third-place finish at a World Cup and their best result in the competition since they lifted the trophy in 1966, improving on fourth-place finishes in 1990 and 2018. For France, beaten by Spain in the semi-final, a tournament that began with genuine ambition ends in fourth place, with a comeback that fell agonisingly short and uncomfortable questions left hanging over a defence that conceded six.

Attention now turns to Sunday's final between Argentina and Spain, with the holders one win from retaining the trophy — and Messi chasing both his own farewell script and a scoring record that, as of Saturday night, is no longer his.
facts: England beat France 6-4 in the 2026 World Cup third-place playoff at Hard Rock Stadium, Miami Gardens, on 18 July 2026 — ten goals, the wildest scoreline of the tournament.

Declan Rice (3'), Ezri Konsa (18') and Bukayo Saka (37', 45+1') put England 4-0 up at half-time; Saka completed his hat-trick from the penalty spot in the 87th minute and Jude Bellingham scored in stoppage time.
Kylian Mbappé scored twice (48', 66') and Ousmane Dembélé added France's fourth deep in stoppage time.
Mbappé's brace took him to ten goals in this tournament, clear at the top of the Golden Boot standings, and to 22 career World Cup goals — passing Lionel Messi's all-time record of 21.
Messi, on eight tournament goals, faces Spain with Argentina in Sunday's final in East Rutherford.
Bronze is England's first World Cup third-place finish and their best result since winning the tournament in 1966.

body: Today's fixture in Ljubljana is, on paper, the least glamorous game Israel's under-20s could have earned: a ninth-place decider against Lithuania, played hours before somebody else's final. Yet it closes a week in which the Israeli basketball pipeline displayed both of its waves at once.

In Las Vegas, three products of the system finished an NBA Summer League fortnight inside NBA organisations. In Slovenia, the current under-20 generation rebuilt a broken tournament with consecutive wins by 25 and 22 points and the competition's eighth-ever triple-double. Neither wave delivered a trophy. Both delivered evidence.

The first wave needs little introduction because this desk profiled it on Friday. The 2018 gold in Chemnitz, won 80–66 over Croatia, and the 2019 defence in Tel Aviv, 92–84 over Spain, made Israel only the second nation at that point to retain the under-20 European title.

Seven summers later, Ben Saraf and Danny Wolf have just completed a Summer League in Brooklyn's rotation, and Emanuel Sharp, taken 45th by Sacramento last month, signed off his own fortnight by leading the Kings' scoring with 16 points in a 92–90 win over Charlotte. Three Israelis wearing NBA practice gear in the same Las Vegas cycle is not an accident of talent; it is what a functioning production line looks like from the far end.

The second wave is the more interesting story precisely because it stumbled first. The 79–66 round-of-16 defeat by Greece exposed a structural fault: Oren Sahar and Rany Belaga supplied 39 of Israel's 66 points, and no third route existed when the first two were smothered.

What followed answered that exact question rather than a more comfortable one. Italy were beaten 84–59 with four scorers in double figures, and Latvia were dismantled 96–74 behind a 26–9 second quarter. Tamir Gold's 25 points led a spread attack, while Belaga converted himself from overloaded scorer into distributor: 16 points, 12 assists, 10 rebounds — the first triple-double by an Israeli at this championship according to Israeli reporting, and only the eighth in the event's history on FIBA's own count.

Honesty requires the first counterpoint immediately: classification wins are not medals. The 2018 team beat France by 26 in a European semi-final; this team beat Latvia by 22 for the right to contest ninth place. The opposition's stakes, depth and desperation are not comparable, and nobody in Israeli basketball should pretend a 9–12 bracket rout carries the developmental information of a knockout win over a contender. The Greece night remains the tournament's truest measurement, and Israel failed it.

The second counterpoint sits one level up. The golden generation's senior translation remains incomplete. At EuroBasket 2025, Israel's best senior tournament in a decade — the first knockout appearance since 2015 — still ended in the round of 16, 84–79 to Greece, with Deni Avdija's 23 points insufficient against Giannis Antetokounmpo's 37.

There is an uncomfortable symmetry in Greece eliminating the seniors in 2025 and the under-20s in 2026. Youth titles have so far produced a senior team that reaches the last 16 and stops there. That is progress from the pre-2018 baseline, not proof the pipeline ends anywhere near a podium.

The third counterpoint belongs to Las Vegas itself. Summer League minutes are not NBA roster spots. Two nights before Sharp's finale, Houston held Saraf to two points in sixteen and a half minutes and forced five turnovers from Wolf, both finishing at minus-15 as Brooklyn missed the semi-final field. Sharp's strong fortnight buys him a training-camp audition, nothing firmer — the distance between a July box score and an October rotation is the widest gap in professional basketball, and Israeli coverage, this desk included, should resist collapsing it.

Weigh all three counterpoints, though, and notice what they have in common: each defines the standard the pipeline has not yet met, and none refutes the direction it is moving. A development system is not judged by whether every cohort wins gold — the 2018–19 group was exceptional and knew it. It is judged by whether the environment keeps producing players who reach the next legitimate test.

By that measure, this month has been quietly emphatic: Division A status preserved for the 2027 age group, three draft-age Israelis absorbed into NBA structures, and a current under-20 captain rewriting his role mid-tournament rather than shrinking inside it.

Which is what today's game against Lithuania actually measures. Not talent — Greece measured that and found it short of the elite. Not history — the Belaga triple-double is already banked. What remains is the least marketable and most predictive trait a programme can show: whether standards hold when the incentives are thin.

Lithuania arrive from a 100–84 win over Poland and will test whether Israel's spread scoring and defensive concentration were a response to relegation danger or a settled identity. Playing a third classification game in five days at full intent, with nothing on offer but the number nine, is the habit that separates a system from a lucky generation.

So the judgement this column lands on is deliberately unromantic. Ninth place is ninth place; it will hang no banners and it should embarrass no one. If Israel win today they finish 5–2, having lost only to the host nation and to Greece, with the fault they carried into the knockout round demonstrably repaired by the players themselves.

That is what the middle of a healthy pipeline looks like between golden peaks: not medals, but a floor that keeps rising while the first wave tests the ceiling somewhere else. The 2018–19 generation showed how high Israeli youth basketball can reach. This week, against smaller stakes and with fewer witnesses, the 2026 group has been showing how far it has become impossible to fall.

title: Helsinki, 19 July 1952: the day Israel walked into the Olympic movement
dek: Seventy-four years ago today, a 25-strong delegation marched behind the blue-and-white flag at the Helsinki Olympic Stadium. Israel's first Olympic Games won no medals — but the debut itself was a quiet act of international recognition for a four-year-old state.

source.name: ILSP Archive Desk
source.originalTitle: From the Archive
source.author: ILSP Sports Desk

verificationSources.label: Olympedia — 1952 Helsinki edition (opening date, nations, athletes, ceremony)
Olympedia — Israel country page (first Games, NOC recognition)

body: On 19 July 1952 — seventy-four years ago today — the Games of the XV Olympiad opened at the Helsinki Olympic Stadium. Finland's president, Juho Kusti Paasikivi, declared the Games open. Paavo Nurmi, the country's greatest distance runner, carried the torch into the arena and lit the flame, before fellow running legend Hannes Kolehmainen kindled a second fire at the top of the stadium tower.

Sixty-nine nations and 4,932 athletes had gathered. Somewhere in that long parade of teams marched a small column of athletes behind a blue-and-white flag that had never before been carried into an Olympic stadium: Israel, competing at the Games for the very first time.

The debut was about far more than sport. The state was barely four years old, born amid the 1948 war that had kept any Israeli team away from the London Games that summer. Olympic historians record the essential point plainly: Israel competed at its first Olympics in 1952 in Helsinki, the same year in which its National Olympic Committee was formally recognised by the International Olympic Committee.

That sequence matters. In the early 1950s, membership of the Olympic family was one of the clearest certificates of normal statehood available to a new country — a stage on which Israel could appear not as a contested political question but as simply one delegation among sixty-nine. Marching in Helsinki was, in its way, a second declaration of independence.

The delegation itself was modest and eclectic: twenty-five athletes — twenty-two men and three women — entered in seventeen events across five sports: athletics, basketball, diving, shooting and swimming. The honour of carrying the flag at the opening ceremony fell to Abraham Shneior, the 23-year-old captain of the national basketball team. Born in Mandatory Palestine and captain of Maccabi Tel Aviv, Shneior embodied the generation for whom the state and its sporting institutions had grown up together.

On the field of play, the results were what one would expect of a tiny, war-scarred country facing the world's best. The basketball team lost its qualification-round matches, falling 47–57 to the Philippines and then, agonisingly, 52–54 to Greece — a two-point margin that separated the debutants from the main tournament — to finish joint twentieth. On the track, sprinter David Tabak battled through to the second-round heats of both the 100 metres and the 200 metres before bowing out.

The man who came closest to the podium was a diver. Yoav Ra'anan, then twenty-four, finished ninth on the three-metre springboard — one place outside the leading group — and twenty-fourth on the platform. His Helsinki showing was no fluke: two years later he won springboard gold and platform silver at the 1954 Asian Games, and he returned to dive for Israel at Melbourne in 1956.
In a delegation of pioneers, Ra'anan was the first Israeli Olympian who could genuinely be discussed in the language of contention rather than mere participation.

The timing gave the debut an added resonance. Helsinki 1952 was the first cold-war Olympics: the Soviet Union, too, was competing at its first Games, and the stadium became a stage on which the new post-war order presented itself to the world. Israel entered the family of Olympic nations at the precise moment that family was being redrawn — and for a state whose very legitimacy was still contested in international forums, the value of being an ordinary name on an extraordinary list is hard to overstate.

No medals came home from Finland, and none would come for another four decades, until Barcelona in 1992. Yet Helsinki endures as one of the most consequential entries in the history of Israeli sport. Every Israeli Olympian since — every judoka, sailor, gymnast and runner who has stood on a podium or simply marched at an opening ceremony — traces a direct line back to that column of twenty-five who walked into the Helsinki rain-grey afternoon of 19 July 1952 and, by walking, made a point no communiqué could: the state was here, and it intended to compete.
facts: The 1952 Helsinki Olympics opened on 19 July 1952, with 69 nations and 4,932 athletes; Finnish president Juho Kusti Paasikivi opened the Games and Paavo Nurmi lit the flame.
Helsinki 1952 was Israel's first Olympic Games, held the same year the IOC formally recognised Israel's National Olympic Committee.
Israel's delegation numbered 25 athletes — 22 men and 3 women — competing in 17 events across five sports: athletics, basketball, diving, shooting and swimming.
Basketball captain Abraham Shneior, of Maccabi Tel Aviv, carried the Israeli flag at the opening ceremony.
Israel's basketball team lost 47–57 to the Philippines and 52–54 to Greece; diver Yoav Ra'anan recorded the best individual placing, ninth on the 3m springboard.
Israel's first Olympic medals came four decades later, at Barcelona 1992.

title: Gadrani doubtful for Larnaca as contract standoff with Beitar Jerusalem sharpens
dek: Beitar's Georgian centre-back is a fitness doubt for Thursday's Conference League opener against AEK Larnaca while pressing for a raise of at least 50 per cent — with the club and player reportedly hundreds of thousands of euros apart, yet both minded to strike a deal this week.
homepageReason: Beitar's first-choice centre-back in doubt for Thursday's European opener while a six-figure contract standoff plays out.

body: Beitar Jerusalem may have to open their European campaign without Luka Gadrani. The Georgian centre-back is doubtful for Thursday's Conference League second-round qualifier, first leg, against AEK Larnaca, according to Israeli reporting on Sunday morning — and the fitness question has landed in the middle of an increasingly public standoff over his salary.

The doubt is medical rather than tactical. Gadrani is working his way back from injury, and head coach Almog Cohen said 'the chances are not high' when asked about him and the club's other injured players ahead of the trip to Cyprus.

He sat out Saturday night's Toto Cup quarter-final against Hapoel Tel Aviv in Netanya, consistent with the team sheets from that tie: he appeared neither in the starting eleven nor among the substitutes used as Beitar drew 2–2 and went out 3–1 on penalties.

The money is where the two Sunday reports diverge, and every figure belongs to its outlet. One has Gadrani earning approximately €250,000 a season and seeking an improvement of at least 50 per cent. The other goes further, reporting that the player's camp has conveyed a demand of €450,000–500,000 net per season, against a Beitar offer stretching to roughly €320,000–350,000.
The outlets disagree on the numbers but agree on the substance: the defender wants a substantially bigger contract, and the club accepts the current terms need reopening.

For all the gap, the tone from both camps is reportedly constructive. Talks are expected to intensify this week, and there is optimism born of both sides' desire to continue the partnership; any new agreement would reportedly run for at least two years.

The same reporting notes how much the coaching staff missed their defensive pairing in Netanya. The view inside the club is that the back line looks different when Gadrani and fellow centre-back Brayan Carabalí are both fit — the two goals conceded, staff were quoted as saying, 'with slightly more concentration, would not have created any threat.'

Gadrani's leverage is easy to trace. The 29-year-old, born in Tbilisi in April 1997, joined Beitar in September 2025 and quickly became a fixture at the heart of the defence; his current deal, in shirt number 44, runs to 30 June 2027.

With two seasons of control remaining, Beitar are under no immediate pressure. But a settled, motivated first-choice centre-back on the eve of a European campaign is worth paying for, and both sides appear to know it.

The calendar now does the squeezing. Beitar open against AEK Larnaca on Thursday 23 July, with the return leg a week later on 30 July — and the coming days will have to resolve both questions at once: whether Gadrani's body is ready for Cyprus, and whether his next contract will be agreed closer to his number or the club's.

title: Josh Kerr shatters athletics' oldest track record with 3:42.66 mile in London
dek: The Scot took nearly half a second off Hicham El Guerrouj's 3:43.13, a mark that had stood since Rome in 1999, in front of 60,000 at the London Diamond League.

source.name: Shvoong (Sport 5 network)
source.originalTitle: היסטוריה בלונדון: ג'וש קר שבר את שיא העולם של אל גרוז' בריצת מייל!
source.author: Shvoong editorial team

verificationSources.label: World Athletics — official meet report (3:42.66, splits, field, meeting records)

body: The oldest record on the men's track ledger finally fell on Saturday evening, when Josh Kerr ran one mile in 3 minutes 42.66 seconds at the London Diamond League meeting. The mark had stood since Hicham El Guerrouj clocked 3:43.13 in Rome on 7 July 1999 — 27 years earlier, an entire generation of milers ago.
Kerr, a 28-year-old from Edinburgh, became the first man ever to break 3:43 for the distance, taking 0.47 seconds off the Moroccan's famous figure in front of a 60,000-strong crowd at London Stadium.

The Emsley Carr Mile was built for history from the gun. Pacemakers Brannon Kidder and Žan Rudolf towed the field through halfway, Kidder passing 400m in 54.75 with Kerr just behind in 55.3. The Scot reached 800m in 1:51.1 and 1,200m in 2:46.39, and when the last pacemaker peeled away he was alone against the clock.
His 1,500m split of 3:27.62 was itself quicker than his lifetime best over that shorter distance — a measure of the pace he was sustaining with a lap still to run.

Over the final 100 metres Kerr visibly strained, but the record never slipped from his grasp. "It is very overwhelming," he said afterwards. "There was a lot of hype... I nearly lost it there at the end, but I got over the line."

The run was the culmination of a campaign his sponsor had branded 'Project 222', a reference to the 222 seconds — three minutes and 42 — that breaking the record demanded. It lowered his own previous mile best of 3:45.34, set in 2024, by almost three seconds.

The depth behind him underlined the quality of the race. American Yared Nuguse, so often Kerr's foil over four laps, was second in 3:45.69, while Britain's Jake Heyward ran a personal best of 3:46.73 for third and Germany's Robert Farken set a national record of 3:46.82 in fourth — four men inside 3:47 in the same mile.
For Kerr, the record crowns a steady accumulation of championship honours: the world 1500m title in Budapest in 2023, Olympic 1500m silver in Paris in 2024 and a world indoor crown in Glasgow.

El Guerrouj's mile mark had long been regarded as one of middle-distance running's untouchable standards, surviving assaults from three Olympic cycles' worth of champions before Saturday night finally brought it down.

The record headlined a meeting thick with fast times. Karsten Warholm ran a meeting record of 46.61 in the 400m hurdles, Julien Alfred stopped the clock at 21.66 for a 200m meeting record, Ja'Kobe Tharp won the 110m hurdles in a meeting-record 12.89, and Cierra Jackson threw a Diamond League discus record of 71.72m — a supporting cast that, on almost any other evening, would have owned the headlines.

title: Datiashvili turns a race-one win into seventh at the ILCA 6 Youth Europeans
dek: Gaya Datiashvili opened the European youth championship in Thessaloniki with a race win and recovered from a start disqualification to finish seventh among Europe's under-19 girls, the best result in a 12-strong Israeli team.

body: Gaya Datiashvili closed the ILCA 6 Youth European Championships in Thessaloniki on Saturday as the seventh-ranked European in an 89-boat girls' fleet, extending a run of top-ten continental finishes that has made the Hapoel Zvulun Acre sailor the most consistent presence in Israel's youth dinghy programme.

The official results place her eighth across the line overall. New Zealand's Chloe Turner, third, raced for the accompanying Open European Trophy rather than the championship itself, which left Datiashvili seventh in the European championship classification.

Her twelve-race series at the Nautical Club of Kalamaria was a study in recovery. She won the opening race outright, then slumped to 35th in the second and was disqualified under the U flag for a premature start in race four — a score she was able to discard.
From there she steadied through qualifying to make the gold fleet, then produced her best sailing of the week at the start of the final series with a third and a race win.

Two heavy scores of 35 and 21 followed before she closed with a tenth and a sixth, ending on 131 net points. In a format with no medal race, that consistency over a dozen starts is what the class rewards.

The championship, sailed from 10 to 18 July in light and moderate winds on the Thermaic Gulf, drew 314 sailors — 89 girls and 225 boys. The girls' title went to the home fleet through Greece's Hermionie Ghicas on 58 net points.

Datiashvili arrived as a genuine contender, having finished fourth at last year's European championship and fourth at the 2025 ILCA 6 Youth Worlds in Los Angeles. Her coaches' assessment after racing was candid: she competed at the front for most of the week, but the mid-series inconsistency and the start disqualification cost her a shot at a first international medal.

The boys' team delivered Israel's other headline result. Yahav Geva, also of Hapoel Zvulun Acre, finished 14th overall in the 225-boat male fleet — the best Israeli placing among the boys — winning two qualifying races and signing off with a second place in the final race of the regatta.

Gal Einav of Hapoel Tel Aviv followed in 18th. Both marks represent a clear step up from Israel's leading boys' finishes of 35th and 40th at the previous edition, in a fleet won by Lithuania's Erik Scheidt.

Rebecca Mantel, the second Israeli girl, took fourth place in the silver fleet, closing her week with a race win in the last start. The delegation of twelve — ten boys and two girls — returns directly to training, with the class youth world championship scheduled for mid-August.

For the Israel Sailing Association, Thessaloniki reinforces the ILCA 6 as the productive middle of its youth pathway. A sailor who has now gone fourth, fourth and seventh at major youth championships in successive seasons is knocking persistently on the door of a podium.

Her series included a race-one win, a U-flag disqualification in race four (her discard) and a gold-fleet race win; the format had no medal race.
The championship was sailed 10-18 July 2026 at the Nautical Club of Kalamaria, Thessaloniki, with 314 entries (89 girls, 225 boys); Greece's Hermionie Ghicas won the girls' title on 58 net points.
Yahav Geva was the leading Israeli boy in 14th of 225, with two qualifying race wins and a 2nd in the final race; Gal Einav finished 18th; Lithuania's Erik Scheidt won the boys' fleet.
Rebecca Mantel, Israel's second girl, finished 4th in the silver fleet, winning the last race; the Israeli team numbered 12 sailors.
Datiashvili was 4th at the previous ILCA 6 Youth Europeans and 4th at the 2025 ILCA 6 Youth Worlds in Los Angeles; the squad's next target is the class youth worlds in mid-August.

title: Eli Ohana bids official farewell: "I have finished my path in football"
dek: The 62-year-old Beitar Jerusalem great and 1988 Cup Winners' Cup winner has ruled out ever returning as a coach or executive, dismissing talk of leading Israel alongside Eyal Berkovic and confirming that broadcasting is now his only place in the game.

source.name: Sport1 / Maariv
source.originalTitle: אלי אוחנה נפרד באופן רשמי: "סיימתי את דרכי"
source.author: Sport1 editorial team

verificationSources.label: English Wikipedia record of Eli Ohana's playing, managerial and executive career
Hebrew Wikipedia record confirming honours, 51 caps and 17 goals, the 1988 Cup Winners' Cup role and the 2017-2022 Beitar chairmanship

body: Eli Ohana, one of the greatest footballers Israel has produced, has formally declared his working life in the game over. Asked on the radio programme he presents on Sunday morning whether he would agree to lead the national team alongside Eyal Berkovic, the 62-year-old closed the door without hesitation. "Me and Berkovic to the Israel national team together? There is no chance — it is of no interest," he said. "In sport and in football I am staying only at the sports channel. I have finished my path in football."

The declaration formalises a retreat that has been under way for some time. Ohana has held no formal post since stepping down as Beitar Jerusalem chairman in May 2022, yet his name has rarely left conversations about vacancies at his old club or on the national-team staff. Sunday's remarks were his most explicit farewell yet: no return as coach, executive or federation figure — only the pundit's chair.

It ends one of the richest careers in Israeli football. Nicknamed "King Ohana", the forward came through Beitar Jerusalem's youth ranks and starred for the club across two spells, from 1980 to 1987 and again from 1991 to 1999. He won four Israeli championships in that time — in 1986-87, 1992-93, 1996-97 and 1997-98 — along with State Cups in 1984-85 and 1985-86.

In between came the achievement that made him a landmark figure for the Israeli game. At KV Mechelen between 1987 and 1990 he won the 1987-88 European Cup Winners' Cup, scoring in the semi-final and setting up the winning goal in the 1-0 final victory over Ajax, to become the first Israeli footballer to win a European club trophy.
He added the 1988 European Super Cup with the Belgian side and received the Bravo Award that same year. Between 1984 and 1997 he scored 17 goals in 51 appearances for Israel.

His second career kept him close to the touchline for two more decades. He managed Beitar Jerusalem and other Israeli clubs, led Israel's under-19 side from 2008 to 2016, took caretaker charge of the senior national team in 2010, sat on the Israel Football Association's executive and served as Beitar chairman from May 2017 to May 2022.

Reflecting on Israel's repeated failure to reach major tournaments, Ohana rejected the idea that coaching was to blame. "I do not think Israel's problem over the years has been the coaches. There have been excellent coaches, both foreign and Israeli," he said. "At the end of the day the players do the work on the pitch — their influence is even greater than the coaches'."

Nor does he expect Berkovic, once a mooted candidate, to take the national job. "If you had said Berko to me three or four years ago, I would have been with you. Today? I am not sure he would go. From what I understand — and I have heard him say it himself — that matter is already behind him."

The farewell came, fittingly, with Ohana still at work: his remarks aired hours before Sunday evening's World Cup final between Argentina and Spain, which he was previewing as a broadcaster, sticking with the Spain tip he has carried since the start of the tournament. The man who took Israeli football to a European final will watch this one from the studio — which, by his own words, is now where his story in the game continues.

As a Beitar Jerusalem forward he won four Israeli championships (1986-87, 1992-93, 1996-97, 1997-98) and two State Cups (1984-85, 1985-86).

With KV Mechelen he won the 1987-88 European Cup Winners' Cup — scoring in the semi-final and assisting the winner in the final against Ajax — becoming the first Israeli footballer to win a European club trophy.
He scored 17 goals in 51 appearances for Israel between 1984 and 1997.
After playing he managed Beitar Jerusalem among other clubs, coached Israel's under-19s from 2008 to 2016, and served as Beitar Jerusalem chairman from May 2017 to May 2022.

title: Israel's under-20s beat Croatia 36:31 to end a 21-year wait for a World Championship place
dek: Trailing 14:17 at half-time in Cluj-Napoca, Israel's reserve team produced a 22:14 second half to take 15th place at the M20 EHF EURO — and with it a first junior World Championship qualification since 2005, with Guy Ran Arman scoring 11 and Loïc Bakasu Bibange 10.

source.name: Sport 5
source.originalTitle: הישג: העתודה בכדוריד עלתה לאליפות העולם
source.author: Sport 5 editorial team

Independent Israeli account confirming the result, scorers and the first-since-2005 qualification

body: Twenty-one years of waiting ended in a near-empty hall in Cluj-Napoca on Sunday lunchtime. Israel's under-20 handball team beat Croatia 36:31 in the 15th-place match of the M20 EHF EURO in Romania, claiming the final ranking position that carries qualification for the age group's World Championship. According to Hebrew-language coverage, it is the first time the side known domestically as the reserve national team has reached the tournament since 2005, with the finals now awaiting in North Macedonia in the summer of 2027.

It was done the hard way. Israel trailed 14:17 at the interval, a scoreline confirmed by the official match record, against opponents from one of Europe's genuine handball powers. What followed was the best half of Israel's tournament: a 22:14 surge after the break turned a three-goal deficit into a five-goal victory, completed barely 48 hours after the same squad had been dismantled 35:23 by Iceland.

The comeback was driven by two players in relentless scoring form. Guy Ran Arman, listed on the official match sheet under the surname Resch Erman, struck 11 goals, and Loïc Bakasu Bibange added ten, the pair accounting for 21 of Israel's 36. Yonatan Pelach contributed five, Adi Cohen four, Asaf Sharon and Ben Gross two apiece, and Uri Cohen and Itamar Goldstein one each.

Behind them, the goalkeeping load was shared. Hebrew-language reports credit Alon Rossabi with six saves at a 33 per cent stop rate, Yehonatan Benshitrit with four, and Eitan Elbaz with three. The win owed nothing to the seven-metre line: the official sheet shows Croatia converted seven of eight penalties while Israel scored just one from two, meaning the 36 goals were built almost entirely from open play. Croatia's Moslavac finished with ten at the other end but found too little support once the second half turned.

The route to this decider was unforgiving. Israel arrived off the back of Friday's heavy defeat to Iceland, fielding a squad the Hebrew coverage had described as shorn of four players, while Croatia dropped into the tie after losing their placement meeting with the host nation. On paper it was a mismatch of pedigrees; on the court, Israel's response after the interval settled it emphatically.

The setting gave little hint of the occasion. The official record logs a 12:00 throw-off at the Horia Demian hall in Cluj-Napoca in front of just 60 spectators, a modest stage for the most consequential result an Israeli age-grade handball team has produced in more than two decades.

The wider arc makes the achievement sweeter still. This tournament brought heavy defeats to Sweden, Romania, Czechia and Iceland around wins over Bosnia and Herzegovina and Poland, and after the Iceland loss the campaign had come down to a single winner-takes-all fixture. The players delivered when only victory would do, and a generation that has spent a fortnight absorbing hard lessons in Romania will now test itself against the world's best junior sides next summer.
facts: Israel beat Croatia 36:31 (half-time 14:17 to Croatia) on 19 July 2026 in the 15th-place match of the M20 EHF EURO, per the official EHF match record (match 089; 12:00 throw-off, Horia Demian hall, Cluj-Napoca, 60 spectators).

Fifteenth place secured qualification for the age group's World Championship; Israeli reports state it is the reserve team's first qualification since 2005 and that the 2027 junior World Championship will be staged in North Macedonia.

Guy Ran Arman (match sheet: Resch Erman, No. 3) scored 11 goals and Loïc Bakasu Bibange (No. 34) 10; Yonatan Pelach added 5, Adi Cohen 4, Asaf Sharon 2, Ben Gross 2, Uri Cohen 1 and Itamar Goldstein 1.
Israeli goalkeeper figures per the Hebrew reports: Alon Rossabi 6 saves (33%), Yehonatan Benshitrit 4 (23%), Eitan Elbaz 3 (30%).
The official sheet shows Croatia converted 7 of 8 seven-metre throws to Israel's 1 of 2; Croatia's top scorer Moslavac finished with 10 goals.
Israel won the second half 22:14 after trailing by three at the interval, two days after losing 35:23 to Iceland.

title: Israeli teenagers clock 2:15.00 to erase 35-year-old 1,000m relay record in Rieti
dek: Nivi Seligmann, Roni Rabinovitz, Koral Tsimbalist and Hila Varsano took nearly five seconds off a national mark that had stood since 1991, closing Israel's European under-18 championships on a record even without a place in the final.

source.name: Sport 5
source.originalTitle: שיא ישראל חדש ב-1,000 מטר שליחות - ערוץ הספורט
source.author: Sport 5 editorial team

verificationSources.label: World Athletics — European U18 Championships 2026 results, day 4 (women's 1,000m medley relay round 1; men's 2,000m steeplechase final)
World Athletics — European U18 Championships 2026 results, day 3 (women's 400m hurdles semi-finals)

body: Israel's under-18 women closed their European championships in Rieti with a national record. Nivi Seligmann, Roni Rabinovitz, Koral Tsimbalist and Hila Varsano ran 2:15.00 in Sunday's opening round of the 1,000m medley relay at the Stadio Raul Guidobaldi — a time confirmed on the official results — to set a new Israeli best over the rarely contested distance.

The mark they beat had stood for 35 years: 2:19.7, set back in 1991. Sunday's quartet stripped almost five seconds off it in a single run of the sprint-medley format, whose legs of 100, 200, 300 and 400 metres were shared out with Seligmann of Leader Netanya leading off, Maccabi Tel Aviv's Rabinovitz and Maccabi Ramat Hasharon's Tsimbalist carrying the middle two legs, and Varsano closing on the 400m.

The record did not come with progression attached. Israel finished seventh in the third heat, 20th of the 24 nations entered, and missed the final in a round where Czechia's 2:07.62 led all qualifiers and every finalist broke 2:10.
For a team assembled from three clubs in an event Israel almost never races, the gap to the leaders reads less as a verdict than as a starting point.

For Varsano, the relay capped a heavy weekend. A day earlier the 17-year-old had run her 400m hurdles semi-final, finishing eighth in the third semi in 1:02.11 to fall short of the final — an entirely forgivable exit two days after a 1:00.02 in the heats had lowered her own Israeli under-18 record.

There was a sharper ending on the infield during the same session. Ido Noam took sixth place in the 2,000m steeplechase final in 5:53.96, delivering exactly the top-eight finish the national federation's professional director had predicted for him.
Aviv Ochman fared tougher in the same race, caught out in a punishing pace and coming home 14th in 6:19.99.
Israel left Rieti with two new national marks to show for the trip — one individual, one shared by four teenagers who had never run faster.
facts: Israel's under-18 women's team of Nivi Seligmann, Roni Rabinovitz, Koral Tsimbalist and Hila Varsano ran 2:15.00 in round 1 of the 1,000m medley relay at the 2026 European Athletics U18 Championships in Rieti on 19 July 2026, confirmed on the official World Athletics results page.
The time is reported as a new Israeli record for the 1,000m relay, beating a 2:19.7 mark that had stood since 1991.
Israel finished seventh in heat 3 and 20th of the 24 nations entered; Czechia led round 1 with 2:07.62.
Hila Varsano finished eighth in her 400m hurdles semi-final on Saturday in 1:02.11 and did not reach the final, after her Israeli U18 record of 1:00.02 in the heats.
Ido Noam finished sixth in the men's 2,000m steeplechase final in 5:53.96; Aviv Ochman was 14th in 6:19.99.
The championships took place at the Stadio Raul Guidobaldi in Rieti, Italy, from 16 to 19 July 2026.
